coverAlt: Light and dark card examples using the same semantic surface and text roles.

title: SVG vs PNG for Website Icons: A Practical Choice
description: Choose an icon format based on scaling, detail, styling and delivery. Compare SVG and PNG, set dimensions, and check sharpness at actual display sizes.
body:
SVG is usually a strong choice for simple scalable interface icons; PNG is useful when the artwork is inherently raster or a destination requires a bitmap. Choose based on the asset’s content and delivery constraints, then inspect the result at its real display size. A larger file is not automatically a sharper or more useful icon.

First identify what you actually have. A file ending in SVG can contain an embedded raster image, and exporting a PNG into an SVG wrapper does not recreate vector geometry. Keep the original editable source when you control it so future exports do not depend on a screenshot.

Compare the requirements

RequirementSVGPNG
Simple shapes at several sizesScales without a fixed pixel gridNeeds sufficient pixel dimensions
Detailed raster textureMay be inefficient or contain a bitmapNatural fit for raster artwork
CSS-driven color inside markupInline paths can use currentColorUsually needs another image or a separate technique
A service requiring a PNG uploadExport a PNG variantUse the requested dimensions

MDN’s image format guide explains SVG’s drawing-based structure and the role of raster formats. File size depends on the actual content. Measure representative exports rather than assuming that every SVG is smaller than every PNG.

Give an SVG a stable drawing area

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
     viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24"
     fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"
     aria-hidden="true">
  <path d="M5 12h14M12 5l7 7-7 7" />
</svg>

This original arrow example uses a viewBox to define the coordinate system and explicit dimensions for its rendered box. As inline markup, its currentColor can follow surrounding CSS. An SVG loaded through an image element does not automatically receive the page’s text color in the same way.

The example is hidden from assistive technology because it is intended to accompany a text label such as “Continue.” If an icon is the only visible content of a control, give the control an accessible name describing its action. Do not expose a technical filename as the label.

Export PNG at the size the display needs

For a 24 CSS pixel icon, a 48-by-48 PNG can supply a two-times-density variant. Retain the intended 24-by-24 layout dimensions. Increasing the source resolution cannot repair artwork that was already blurred before export, so generate the bitmap from the original source.

<img src="/assets/action-24.png"
     srcset="/assets/action-48.png 2x"
     width="24" height="24" alt="">

Use this pattern only when the two files represent the same artwork at the stated densities. If the image conveys meaning by itself, provide useful alternative text. When a nearby visible label already communicates the same action, an empty alternative prevents redundant announcement.

Check the icon in context

Inspect the asset at 16, 20 and 24 CSS pixels, or at the sizes your interface actually uses. Very thin strokes and small gaps may become indistinct even with a vector format. Sometimes a simplified small-size version is more effective than scaling a detailed large illustration down.

Test light and dark surfaces, disabled treatment and focus states. Confirm that an icon beside text aligns optically with the label rather than merely sharing the same bounding-box height. Also check that the control’s clickable area is not limited to the small visible drawing.

Prepare an asset record for handoff

Record the source file, export variants, intended display dimensions, color behavior and whether the asset is decorative or meaningful. Keep supplied assets within your permitted usage and avoid treating a visible website file as an automatically reusable brand resource.

For a practical handoff, include one example in a real button and one on each supported theme surface. The button-state guide covers the surrounding interaction requirements, while the handoff checklist helps preserve those decisions for implementation.
coverAlt: A vector arrow beside a deliberately pixelated arrow demonstrating vector geometry and raster pixels.

title: Accessible Button States: Default, Focus and Disabled
description: Specify buttons beyond the default screenshot. Cover keyboard focus, hover, pressed and disabled behavior with native HTML and a practical review matrix.
body:
An accessible button specification includes its purpose, label, keyboard behavior and states, not only its default appearance. Begin with a native button for an action and define what happens before, during and after activation. A link remains the appropriate element when the primary purpose is navigation.

Use a small review matrix for every important action. The matrix turns vague feedback such as “make it accessible” into concrete checks that a designer and developer can perform on the same component.

Specify states separately

StateWhat to define
DefaultLabel, dimensions, colors and action
HoverPointer feedback without hiding essential information
Keyboard focusPersistent visible indicator and clear location
PressedFeedback while activation occurs
DisabledWhy the action is unavailable and how it behaves
Busy or completedProgress, duplicate-action handling and result feedback

The ARIA button pattern documents button semantics and keyboard expectations. Native HTML supplies much of this behavior; replacing a button with a clickable generic element creates more work and more ways to miss an interaction.

Build from a native control

<button class="action" type="button">
  Save changes
</button>
.action {
  min-height: 2.75rem;
  padding: .65rem 1rem;
  border: 1px solid transparent;
  border-radius: .75rem;
  background: #183224;
  color: #ffffff;
  font: inherit;
}
.action:hover:not(:disabled) { background: #244b35; }
.action:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #155eef;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
.action:disabled { opacity: .6; }

This is an illustrative starting point, not a complete component library. Test the outline against every adjacent surface and confirm that ancestors do not clip it. The focus-visible criterion explains why sighted keyboard users need to know where interaction will occur.

The example’s height is a design choice. WCAG 2.2’s minimum target-size criterion generally uses 24 by 24 CSS pixels, with specified exceptions including spacing. Do not treat a tiny visible icon as the whole target when a larger button box can make the action easier to use.

Choose disabled behavior intentionally

A native disabled button suppresses activation and is normally removed from sequential keyboard focus. If users need to understand why the action is unavailable, provide a visible explanation near the relevant controls. A tooltip available only on hover is a weak place for essential instructions.

Using aria-disabled="true" communicates a disabled state but does not itself suppress activation or apply visual treatment. MDN’s aria-disabled reference explains the implementation responsibilities. Choose that pattern only when you deliberately need its behavior, then guard mouse and keyboard activation in code.

Account for work in progress

For an asynchronous save, decide whether repeated activation should be prevented, which label appears during the request and where success or failure is communicated. Preserve enough context for a user to understand what changed. If the request fails, make the retry path available and explain the problem near the relevant interface.

A spinner alone is not a complete status message. Keep the action’s meaning clear and consider how updates are announced to assistive technology. Avoid replacing a concise label with a symbol that only makes sense to someone watching the animation.

Run the interaction check

Tab to the button, activate it with the expected keyboard inputs, and follow the resulting focus behavior. Repeat with a long label, enlarged text and the dark theme. Confirm that a disabled action cannot be triggered through another input path.

Finally, review label contrast and focus visibility using the contrast guide. Save the state matrix beside the component examples. That record gives later edits a clear standard for preserving behavior as well as appearance.
coverAlt: Four illustrative save buttons in default, hover, keyboard focus and disabled states.

title: A Design Handoff Checklist Developers Can Verify
description: Hand off a website with clear tokens, assets, responsive rules and interaction states. Use acceptance criteria that can be checked in the running interface.
body:
A useful design handoff tells the developer what should happen, which details are fixed, and how to verify the result. Screenshots help establish visual intent, but they do not explain responsive behavior, focus states, asset variants or what to do when content changes. Pair the reference with a small set of observable acceptance criteria.

Start by naming the pages and components included in the handoff. Separate approved decisions from open questions. If a team has only reviewed the homepage, avoid presenting the resulting notes as a complete product-wide design system.

1. Record the reference conditions

FieldExample to adapt
Page and statePricing page, annual option selected
ViewportNarrow, middle and wide reference widths
ThemeLight and dark where supported
ContentRealistic titles, prices and error messages
Source of truthDesign file version and implementation branch

Use real or clearly labeled example content. A layout reviewed with three short words can fail when a real product name wraps. Include at least one long-content case for navigation, cards and buttons so implementation decisions are made before the final review.

2. Deliver tokens with their roles

Provide the active typography, color, spacing, radius and elevation values. Explain what each semantic token controls and identify exceptions. A developer should know whether a value is an intentional rule or a measurement from one reference screenshot.

For an existing website, use the design-system inventory workflow to separate observation from inference. If the implementation uses CSS variables or Tailwind, include the intended mapping rather than leaving a second round of naming decisions to the recipient.

3. List assets and their behavior

Include the editable asset source where appropriate, export variants, intended dimensions and relevant usage permissions. State whether each icon is decorative or conveys meaning. Identify logos or illustrations that need a different treatment on dark backgrounds.

For fonts, record the actual family, required weights, fallback stack and delivery location. Avoid asking the developer to infer a font from a screenshot when a source file or known family name is available. Link to the icon-format guide when export choices need explanation.

4. Describe responsive and interactive behavior

Specify which layouts wrap, stack, scroll locally or change navigation mode. For important controls, include default, hover, keyboard focus, disabled, loading and error states as applicable. State where focus should go after a dialog opens or an action changes the page.

Chrome’s device-mode documentation provides a useful way to inspect viewport changes, while noting the limits of simulation. Add a real-device check for interactions or performance concerns that emulation cannot settle.

5. Write acceptance criteria as observable outcomes

Component: guide card
- A long title wraps without overlapping the category label.
- The entire page fits a 320 CSS pixel viewport.
- The cover keeps its intended aspect ratio.
- The link has a visible keyboard focus indicator.
- Light and dark text/surface pairs are checked separately.
- The card remains usable when text is enlarged.

Open question:
- Should every card be equal height when summaries vary?

Avoid criteria such as “looks premium” without a reference or an observable meaning. A specific statement like “title and button do not overlap at narrow widths” can be checked and resolved. Keep subjective design feedback, factual defects and open product decisions distinguishable.

6. Review the running implementation

Compare representative pages at the agreed widths, then interact with them. Review keyboard focus, longer content, missing images and error states. WCAG’s reflow guidance is a useful reference for checking content access as the layout narrows, rather than judging only a fixed desktop image.

Record each issue with the page, state, expected result and observed result. Assign an owner to unresolved questions. When a decision changes, update the specification as well as the implementation so the two do not drift apart.

For an AI-assisted build, put the reviewed decisions into a DESIGN.md brief and explicitly direct the coding tool to read it. The checklist remains the human-readable acceptance record: it tells everyone what evidence is needed before the handoff is complete.
coverAlt: A design handoff checklist covering tokens, assets, responsive behavior, interaction states and acceptance checks.

title: CSS Container Queries: Make Cards Fit Their Own Space
description: Build reusable cards that adapt to their container instead of the viewport. Set up containment, choose a useful breakpoint and debug queries that do not apply.
body:
Use a size container query when a component should respond to the space its parent gives it. A card in a sidebar can remain compact while the same card in the main column uses a horizontal layout, even though both appear in the same browser window. A viewport breakpoint alone cannot distinguish those two situations.

Start with a readable stacked card. The query should enhance that working layout when sufficient space becomes available. This makes the component easier to reuse and gives you a sensible baseline if a target environment does not support the enhancement.

Give the query a separate container

<div class="story-slot">
  <article class="story-card">
    <img src="/images/story.webp" width="640" height="360" alt="A studio workspace">
    <div><h2>Inside the studio</h2><p>Story summary goes here.</p></div>
  </article>
</div>
.story-slot { container: story / inline-size; }
.story-card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }
.story-card img { width: 100%; height: auto; }
@container story (min-width: 34rem) {
  .story-card {
    grid-template-columns: 12rem minmax(0, 1fr);
    align-items: start;
  }
}

The wrapper establishes the named inline-size container, and the query styles its descendant card. Do not expect the card to query its own size simply because you put containment on that same element. MDN’s container query guide explains containment, names and size queries.

Choose the threshold from the content

The 34rem threshold is an example, not a device category. Narrow the card’s slot until the side-by-side layout becomes uncomfortable, then choose a threshold that preserves readable copy and a useful image. Repeat with a longer title before accepting the value.

PlacementExpected behavior
Narrow sidebarImage above the text
Wide main columnImage and text side by side
Wide window with a narrow nested slotStill stacked
Long title at the thresholdWraps without pushing the image out

This test distinguishes the new component rule from the page-level layout. The page decides how much space a slot receives; the card decides how to use it. Keep those responsibilities separate instead of adding a new viewport breakpoint for every place the card appears.

Debug a query that never activates

Inspect the wrapper’s actual width, its computed container properties and the query name. Then check that the target is a descendant of the intended container. A wide browser does not imply that a sidebar container has crossed the threshold.

If the wrapper becomes unexpectedly small, review the surrounding layout and intrinsic sizing. Containment affects sizing behavior, so it should not be added indiscriminately to every element. Give the slot a clear place in its parent grid or flex layout, and use the overflow checklist when content refuses to shrink.

Keep global preferences separate

A component width query is not a replacement for every media query. System color preferences, reduced motion and page-wide navigation changes have different scopes. Choose the query mechanism that describes the decision you are making.

Document one narrow and one wide card example in the handoff. Include the container name, the threshold and the reason the layout changes there. Test the component in two simultaneous placements before calling it reusable: that is the situation where container queries provide the clearest benefit.
coverAlt: A narrow stacked card and a wider side-by-side card responding to their own containers.

title: Position Sticky Not Working? Check These Constraints
description: Debug sticky headers and sidebars by checking offsets, scrolling ancestors, available height and stacking. Fix the constraint instead of switching blindly to fixed.
body:
When position: sticky does not work, check the offset, the scrolling ancestor and the space available for movement. A sticky element remains constrained by its surrounding layout. Changing its z-index will not fix a missing offset or a parent that leaves it nowhere to travel.

Choose one repeatable scroll position and observe what actually happens. Does the element never stick, stick inside an unexpected panel, disappear behind another surface, or stop earlier than you intended? Those symptoms point to different causes.

Start with an explicit offset

.contents {
  position: sticky;
  top: 5rem;
  align-self: start;
}

At least one inset on the sticking axis needs a non-auto value. Here, the example offset leaves room above a table of contents. The position reference explains how sticky positioning relates to the nearest scrolling ancestor and containing block.

Do not copy the 5rem value without checking your header. A header that grows when navigation wraps can cover the top of the sidebar. Define the offset from the actual layout requirements and test enlarged text, not only the default desktop screenshot.

Identify the scrolling ancestor

Inspect ancestors for overflow settings. Values such as auto, scroll and hidden can establish the scrolling mechanism relevant to sticky positioning, even when that ancestor is not the area you expected to scroll. A wrapper added to clip a decorative effect can therefore change sticky behavior.

SymptomInspect
Never starts stickingComputed position and non-auto inset
Sticks inside a small panelAncestor overflow and scroll area
Stops at the end of a short wrapperContaining block height
Covered by another elementStacking and surface treatment
Bottom controls become unreachableSticky element height and viewport space

Temporarily change one suspected ancestor in DevTools to confirm the cause. Then decide whether its overflow behavior is needed. Removing clipping everywhere can create a different layout defect; the durable fix may be to move the clipping to a dedicated child wrapper.

Check height and stretching

A sidebar that is as tall as its containing region has little useful room to move. In a grid or flex arrangement, inspect whether stretching has made the sticky item taller than its content. The example’s start alignment can help when that is the actual cause, but it is not a universal repair for every sticky layout.

Also test a long table of contents. If it is taller than the visible area, users may struggle to reach its lower links. Depending on the design, let it return to normal flow on short screens or give it a deliberate, usable local scroll region. Verify keyboard access before choosing the latter.

Distinguish positioning from visibility

If the element sticks but appears behind content, investigate stacking contexts and backgrounds. Give the sticky region a suitable surface when content passes behind it. A larger z-index can address an ordering problem only within the relevant stacking relationships; it does not change the scroll constraint.

Use fixed positioning only when you actually want an element removed from normal document flow and anchored according to fixed-position behavior. Substituting fixed for sticky can introduce overlap, require compensating space and change how the element behaves near the end of its section.

Verify the whole scroll path

Test the beginning, middle and end of the containing section, then repeat at a narrow width and with larger text. Tab through links while the sidebar is stuck. Record the responsible ancestor or sizing rule alongside the fix so a later layout refactor does not quietly recreate the problem.
coverAlt: A sticky sidebar within a tall page region, with a visible top offset and the containing boundary.

title: Unitless Line Height in CSS: Why Inheritance Matters
description: Choose readable line spacing and understand unitless inheritance. Compare number and length values, inspect nested text, and test user spacing overrides.
body:
A unitless line height is a multiplier applied to the element’s own font size. That makes it useful for text whose size changes across nested elements or responsive layouts. A computed length can instead be inherited as the same distance, creating cramped lines when a child uses larger text.

Begin with the reading task: a paragraph, heading and compact control do not need identical spacing. Establish a body-text baseline, then review other roles with their actual fonts and content. A single number is not a substitute for looking at several lines of real text.

Compare two inheritance patterns

.unitless-parent { font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.5; }
.length-parent { font-size: 16px; line-height: 24px; }
.large-child { font-size: 24px; }

If the child inherits the unitless value, its used line height is 36px. If it inherits the 24px length, that inherited distance remains 24px. This example isolates inheritance; other inline content and layout details can still influence a line box. MDN’s line-height reference explains the value types and their computed behavior.

ExampleResult to inspect
16px text with 1.5A 24px used line height
24px child inheriting 1.5A 36px used line height
24px child inheriting 24pxThe same 24px length
Mixed text and inline iconsAlignment and the resulting line box

Set typography roles deliberately

body { font-size: 1rem; line-height: 1.6; }
.article-title { line-height: 1.15; }
.field-label { line-height: 1.4; }
.article-copy { max-width: 65ch; }

These are starting values for review, not accessibility certification. A long reading column may need more comfortable spacing than a short display heading. Font metrics also matter: inspect ascenders, descenders, accents and punctuation using the actual loaded typeface.

Compare the same paragraph at a narrow and wide line measure. If it is difficult to follow across the page, consider the width as well as line height. Adding more space between lines cannot fully compensate for an unsuitable font size or an excessively wide reading column.

Do not use line height as a button-sizing shortcut

A control sized entirely by a large fixed line height may look centered with one short label and fail when the label wraps. Prefer explicit padding and an appropriate minimum size, then let text occupy the height it needs. Check the component with a longer translated label or a larger default font.

Likewise, separate paragraph spacing from line spacing. Margins or a parent layout gap control the distance between blocks; line height governs spacing within the text. Keeping these responsibilities distinct makes the spacing system easier to change without damaging reading rhythm.

Allow user spacing changes

WCAG’s text-spacing criterion concerns preserving content and functionality when users override spacing. It is not a command that every design must ship with all of the criterion’s test values. Avoid fixed-height text containers and clipping that cause information to disappear under those overrides.

Test larger line, word, letter and paragraph spacing together on a representative page. Inspect navigation, cards, form labels and error messages as well as body copy. A paragraph may adapt correctly while a compact card footer clips its final line.

Capture the decision in the type specification

Record font family, weight, size, line height and intended reading width as one role. Include a multi-line example instead of only an alphabet specimen. If the result differs between environments, use the rendered-font workflow before adjusting spacing around what might be a fallback font.
coverAlt: Two typography examples showing a unitless 1.5 multiplier producing 24 and 36 pixel line heights for different text sizes.

title: Object Fit Cover vs Contain: Fix Website Image Cropping
description: Choose cover or contain based on what an image must preserve. Define the image box, adjust the focal point and test portrait, landscape and transparent assets.
body:
Use object-fit: cover when an image should fill its box and cropping is acceptable. Use contain when the entire image must remain visible, even if that leaves empty space. First define the box: changing object-fit alone will not establish the layout dimensions you want.

A product photograph, logo and editorial portrait have different requirements. Decide what information must survive before selecting a crop strategy. Keeping a uniform row of thumbnails is useful only if the thumbnails still communicate their subjects.

Separate the image box from its content

.story-image {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 4 / 3;
  object-fit: cover;
  object-position: 50% 35%;
}

The width and aspect ratio establish the rendered box in this example. Cover then scales the image content to fill it, preserving the content’s proportions while cropping excess. The position shifts which part remains visible. See the object-fit reference for the behavior of cover, contain and fill.

Asset and purposeStarting choiceReview concern
Editorial thumbnailCoverFace or subject cut off
Logo in a partner listContainEnough contrast around transparent areas
Screenshot with important edge labelsContainText remains readable
Decorative full-bleed photographCoverCrop still supports the composition

The default fill behavior can distort content when both dimensions force a different aspect ratio. If a circle in the source becomes an oval, inspect sizing and fitting before searching for a higher-resolution file. More pixels will not fix geometric stretching.

Give contained assets an intentional surface

.partner-logo {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: 7rem;
  object-fit: contain;
  padding: 1rem;
  box-sizing: border-box;
  background: #ffffff;
}

This example creates a consistent logo area without cropping the mark. The white surface is a design choice that must fit the supplied artwork and surrounding theme. Inspect transparent edges and marks with white lettering; a technically uncropped logo can still be invisible on the wrong background.

Adjust the focal point with evidence

Start with the center and compare the image at every required shape. For a portrait, move the visible region toward the face if the crop loses it. The object-position property controls alignment within the element’s box; it does not understand what the important subject is.

When one crop cannot serve both a wide hero and a small portrait card, prepare an alternate composition. A carefully chosen source variant is often better than extreme positioning. Record the focal point or alternate asset alongside the content so the decision survives a future template change.

Do not confuse cropping with delivery size

Object-fit changes presentation, not the number of bytes in the downloaded image. A small thumbnail can still fetch a very large original. Use srcset and sizes to provide suitable resolution candidates, and use cropping rules to control their appearance.

Likewise, width and height attributes can help communicate the image’s intrinsic proportions, but they do not replace a deliberate crop specification. Inspect the final computed dimensions and test loading before assuming that the intended space is reserved.

Run a small asset matrix

Test a landscape image, portrait image, square image and transparent mark in the same component. Add a missing-image case and a long caption. Check desktop and mobile crops, then confirm rounded clipping does not hide controls or meaningful text. Save the chosen fit, position, ratio and source variants as one reusable media specification.
coverAlt: Illustrative contain and cover boxes showing the whole scene with empty space versus a cropped scene filling its box.

title: CSS Logical Properties: Layouts That Follow Text Direction
description: Replace direction-dependent spacing with logical CSS properties. Understand inline and block axes, test RTL content, and preserve intentional physical placement.
body:
Logical CSS properties describe layout relative to the writing mode and direction. They help a component keep a “start” edge or consistent inline padding when text direction changes. Use them where the design follows reading flow, while retaining physical coordinates for effects that intentionally belong to a fixed side.

Start with a simple notice or navigation item rather than mechanically replacing every occurrence of left and right in a large stylesheet. A focused component makes it easier to see which relationships should adapt and which should remain unchanged.

Understand inline and block axes

In ordinary horizontal English text, the inline axis runs across the line and the block axis runs through successive lines. Changing direction changes the start and end of the inline flow; vertical writing modes also change how the axes map to physical dimensions. MDN’s logical properties guide explains these mappings.

Physical habitFlow-relative alternative
padding-left and padding-rightpadding-inline
margin-top and margin-bottommargin-block in horizontal writing
A border on the reading-start edgeborder-inline-start
Left-aligned reading contenttext-align: start
Width along the text lineinline-size

The alternatives express intent rather than serving as universal text substitutions. For example, physical width and inline size are equivalent in a horizontal writing mode but represent different physical dimensions when the writing mode changes.

Build a direction-aware notice

.notice {
  border-inline-start: .25rem solid #0f7fff;
  padding-block: 1rem;
  padding-inline: 1.25rem;
  margin-block: 1.5rem;
  text-align: start;
}
.notice-title { margin-block: 0 .5rem; }

Place this component in both a left-to-right context and a context marked with dir="rtl". The accent border should follow the reading-start edge without a second rule that manually moves it to the other side. Use meaningful content in each context when reviewing the actual experience.

Use layout gaps for sibling spacing

For an icon and label, a flex or grid gap usually describes their separation more clearly than a margin added to one physical side of the icon. Confirm source order and alignment first. Adding row-reverse just to fix a spacing problem can alter the visual order without addressing the underlying structure.

Keep the document’s semantic order sensible for the intended reading sequence. Logical properties do not translate text, resolve every bidirectional-content issue or automatically mirror directional graphics. Review arrows, progress indicators and mixed text such as identifiers as separate content decisions.

Watch for conflicting declarations

During a migration, an older physical margin and a newer logical margin can affect the same edge. Inspect the computed result and the winning declaration rather than assuming the logical version always takes precedence. Remove obsolete rules once you have verified the intended replacement.

Change a small family of related properties at a time. For example, migrate the notice’s accent edge and padding together, then test it before changing all navigation spacing. This keeps a directionality repair from becoming a difficult-to-review site-wide restyling.

Define what should not mirror

A decorative light source or a background illustration may intentionally remain in the same physical position. Record that choice. The goal is to follow the content’s direction where appropriate, not to reverse every visible feature of the page.

Finish with a component matrix covering both directions, long labels, nested content and narrow widths. Add the result to the handoff checklist. A successful migration has an understandable flow-relative rule and clear exceptions, rather than two increasingly different stylesheets for the same component.
coverAlt: Two notices showing the accent border at the reading-start edge in left-to-right and right-to-left layouts.

title: Responsive Images: How srcset and sizes Work Together
description: Serve suitable image resolutions with srcset and sizes. Match the declared image slot to your layout, reserve space and verify the selected resource in Chrome.
body:
Use srcset to offer image candidates and sizes to describe the rendered slot when those candidates use width descriptors. The browser chooses a resource using that information and its environment. CSS still determines the actual layout; an inaccurate sizes value can lead to an unnecessarily large or insufficiently detailed download.

Begin with one component and one source image. Create several resized versions with the same composition, and record each file’s actual pixel width. Do not label a 640px image as 1200w simply because you want the browser to treat it as a larger option.

Match a full-width article image

<img
  src="/images/studio-1200.webp"
  srcset="/images/studio-400.webp 400w,
          /images/studio-800.webp 800w,
          /images/studio-1200.webp 1200w"
  sizes="(max-width: 799px) calc(100vw - 32px), 768px"
  width="1200" height="675"
  alt="A worktable with drawing tools beside a window">

This example assumes 16px page padding on each side below 800px and a 768px image slot above that width. The CSS must implement those assumptions. MDN’s responsive images guide explains width descriptors, density descriptors and how sizes conditions are evaluated.

.article-media {
  width: calc(100% - 32px);
  max-width: 768px;
  margin-inline: auto;
}
.article-media img { display: block; width: 100%; height: auto; }

Place the image inside this wrapper for the example layout. In a real site, the surrounding article container may already provide padding and a maximum width. Adapt the sizes expression to that container instead of adding a second wrapper that changes the intended design.

Account for screen density

Rendered slotIllustrative densityApproximate resource width
384 CSS px1x384 pixels
384 CSS px2x768 pixels
768 CSS px1x768 pixels
768 CSS px2x1536 pixels

The table illustrates resolution needs, not a promise that a particular file is always selected. With the supplied candidates, the last case has no 1536px option. Decide whether a larger export is worthwhile for your artwork, audience and delivery budget after examining the visual result.

Reserve the image’s space

Supply accurate intrinsic dimensions and preserve the intended ratio in CSS. Reserving space helps prevent surrounding content from jumping when an image loads. Google’s layout-shift guidance describes missing image dimensions as one common source of instability.

For a cropped thumbnail, the destination ratio may intentionally differ from the source ratio. Treat that as a separate presentation decision and specify it consistently. The object-fit guide covers how to fill or contain an image within that box.

Verify the browser’s choice

Reload at a representative viewport with DevTools open, inspect the image request and compare its width with the rendered slot. Check another viewport and a higher-density device or emulation setting. Browsers may reuse a previously fetched larger candidate, so shrinking a warm page is not a reliable proof that the smaller candidate is wrong.

Use picture-based art direction when a different composition is required, rather than asking resolution candidates to serve incompatible crops. Finish by recording the component’s slot assumptions, candidate widths and actual loading check. That record makes later layout changes easier to reconcile with the image markup.
coverAlt: Three illustrative image candidates labeled 400w, 800w and 1200w above a separate rendered-slot description.

title: Z-Index Not Working? Trace the Stacking Context
description: Debug a menu hidden behind another component. Trace ancestor stacking contexts, distinguish clipping from layering and repair the relevant stacking boundary.
keyword: z index not working stacking context
body:
A larger z-index does not guarantee that a dropdown will appear above the whole page. It orders the element within its stacking context. If that context sits below a neighboring component, the dropdown cannot escape simply by changing 20 to 999999. Find the boundary that separates the overlapping elements before choosing a new number.

Reproduce the conflict with two siblings

<header class="site-header">
  <div class="menu-panel">Menu content</div>
</header>
<main class="page">Page content</main>
.site-header { position: relative; z-index: 1; }
.menu-panel { position: absolute; z-index: 100; }
.page { position: relative; z-index: 2; }

Where these boxes overlap, the page’s context is above the header’s context. The menu’s 100 is local to the header. Raising the header to 3 changes the relevant comparison; raising only the menu does not. The numbers in this example are illustrative layer assignments, not a universal scale for every application.

MDN’s stacking context guide lists context creators, including certain positioned elements, transforms and opacity below 1. A transform added for animation can therefore change layering even when no new z-index appears beside it.

Inspect both ancestor chains

Select the hidden panel, then its ancestors, and record which ones establish contexts. Repeat for the element covering it. Find the first level where the two chains can be compared. This is more reliable than searching only the panel’s component stylesheet, because the decisive property may belong to a layout wrapper.

EvidenceUseful next step
Panel is behind a siblingCompare their ancestor contexts.
Panel is cut off at an exact edgeInspect overflow and clipping on ancestors.
Panel looks translucentCheck opacity and overlays before changing layer order.
Problem begins during animationInspect transforms and animated ancestor properties.

Temporarily disabling a suspected property in DevTools is a diagnostic step. If removing a transform fixes the menu, check why that transform exists before deleting it from source. The component may still need its animation or positioning behavior.

Choose a repair with a clear owner

For a header-owned dropdown, a deliberate header layer may be enough. For an overlay shared across unrelated sections, a dedicated overlay location can simplify the hierarchy. Moving markup also changes inheritance, positioning and event assumptions, so review those alongside the visual fix. Native modal dialogs use the top layer; treat that as a different mechanism, not another huge z-index value.

Create a small layer inventory for the page: ordinary content, navigation, floating controls and modal UI. Test the repaired menu near a sticky sidebar and at a narrow viewport. Then close it and confirm that it no longer intercepts clicks. A completed layering fix should explain which context changed and why, rather than leaving a collection of escalating numbers behind.
coverAlt: Two parent stacking contexts with a high-numbered child remaining inside the lower parent layer.

title: CSS Margin Collapse: Why Vertical Gaps Look Wrong
description: Understand collapsing block margins with a small worked example. Separate sibling spacing from parent padding and choose a repair that matches the layout.
body:
Two vertical margins do not always add together. In normal block layout, adjoining positive margins can collapse to the larger value. A 24px bottom margin followed by a 16px top margin can produce a 24px gap, not 40px. This behavior often explains why a copied spacing value looks wrong even though DevTools shows the expected declaration.

Measure a minimal block stack

<div class="copy-stack">
  <p class="first">First paragraph</p>
  <p class="second">Second paragraph</p>
</div>
.first { margin: 0 0 24px; }
.second { margin: 16px 0 0; }

Use a plain block wrapper for this test. Adding flex or grid to the wrapper changes the rules you are investigating. Put a background on each paragraph and inspect the distance between their border boxes. The highlighted margin values alone do not tell you whether their combined space is additive.

The MDN margin-collapse reference also covers parent/child and empty-block cases. Negative margins have different combination rules; do not extend the “take the larger value” shortcut to a mix of positive and negative margins.

Distinguish inside space from outside space

If a heading’s top margin seems to push an entire colored section downward, inspect the section’s first in-flow child. Without a separating border, padding or other qualifying content, a parent and first child can share a collapsed margin. Adding more margin to that heading may move the section instead of creating the inset you intended.

.notice {
  padding-block: 24px;
  padding-inline: 20px;
  background: #eef4ff;
}
.notice > :first-child { margin-block-start: 0; }
.notice > :last-child { margin-block-end: 0; }

Here the notice owns its interior padding. The first and last content margins are reset so the boundary spacing has one owner. Keep paragraph spacing inside the notice in your ordinary type rules. This makes the component easier to inspect because outer placement and inner breathing room are explicit.

Use a stack layout when every gap should match

.stack { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 24px; }
.stack > * { margin-block: 0; }

This is a separate layout choice for a component list, not a necessary rewrite of all article prose. Flex items do not collapse their margins, and gap provides the spacing between them. If your goal is only to contain child margins within a block, consider a new formatting context such as flow-root; it does not turn all sibling margins into additive gaps.

Review the first item, a middle pair and the last item after changing the layout. Then test a one-item stack and an empty state. Record which component owns padding and which parent owns inter-item spacing in your spacing system. That ownership decision prevents the same gap from being applied twice later.
coverAlt: A 24 pixel bottom margin and 16 pixel top margin producing one illustrative 24 pixel collapsed gap.

title: Align Card Titles and Footers with CSS Subgrid
description: Use row subgrid to align card sections across a collection without fixed text heights. Build a fallback and test long titles, missing content and narrow layouts.
body:
Use row subgrid when neighboring cards should share the same title, body and footer tracks. Independent nested grids cannot coordinate those interior row sizes. A fixed heading height may appear to solve the problem until a longer title or larger text arrives. Subgrid lets the parent grid coordinate the rows while each card keeps its own markup.

Give every card the same section structure

<div class="cards">
  <article class="card">
    <h2>Short title</h2>
    <p>A concise description.</p>
    <a href="/guide-a/">Read guide A</a>
  </article>
  <article class="card">
    <h2>A longer title that wraps onto another line</h2>
    <p>Another description.</p>
    <a href="/guide-b/">Read guide B</a>
  </article>
</div>
.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 18rem), 1fr));
  gap: 1.25rem;
}
.card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; padding: 1.25rem; }
.card > * { margin: 0; }
@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) {
  .card { grid-row: span 3; grid-template-rows: subgrid; }
}

The baseline is an ordinary readable card grid. The enhancement makes each card span three parent rows and reuse those tracks internally. The example links are placeholders for your actual routes. Use real destinations when adapting the markup.

MDN’s subgrid guide explains track sharing and inherited gaps. Only the selected axis becomes a subgrid here: the cards share rows, while the parent still decides how many card columns fit.

Stress the alignment with content

Compare a one-line title with a three-line title in the same visual row of cards. Their body sections should begin on the shared next track. Then add a long description and inspect where the footers land. This reveals the actual benefit more clearly than three cards with identical placeholder text.

Keep the three-section contract explicit. If an image becomes a fourth direct child, update the track span and placement strategy. If a description is optional, preserve an intentional slot or define explicit grid placement; silently removing a child can shift the footer into the wrong row. Avoid empty filler text just to force an alignment.

CaseExpected review
Two cards with different title lengthsBody sections begin on the same shared track.
One card at a narrow widthContent reads in its original order.
Description omittedFooter remains in its intended section.
Larger textRows grow without clipped copy.

Decide whether coordination is actually wanted

Shared tracks trade compactness for alignment. A long description can create space in its neighboring card, which may be desirable in a comparison grid and unnecessary in a news feed. Check real content before applying subgrid to every card on the site.

Finish by documenting the section count, fallback behavior and expected alignment at each layout. Keep DOM order logical and let the grid handle presentation. This gives the next developer a concrete contract to maintain when adding badges, metadata or a second action.
coverAlt: Two cards with different title lengths sharing aligned body and footer rows through subgrid.

title: CSS Aspect Ratio: Size the Box Before Fitting the Image
description: Use aspect-ratio for consistent media slots. Understand automatic dimensions, content constraints and the separate role of object-fit with practical CSS examples.
body:
The aspect-ratio property describes a box’s preferred width-to-height relationship. It is useful for a responsive media slot whose width comes from its container and whose height should follow a consistent proportion. It does not decide which part of an image remains visible; that is a separate fitting and cropping choice.

Start with one automatic dimension

.preview-slot {
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  background: #eef2f7;
}
.preview-slot img {
  display: block;
  width: 100%;
  height: 100%;
  object-fit: contain;
}

Place the image inside the preview slot. At 640px wide, an unconstrained 16:9 slot is 360px high. At 320px wide, it is 180px high. These are arithmetic examples, not measurements of a specific screen. Use contain for a product screenshot that must remain fully visible, or choose an intentional crop for editorial photography.

MDN’s aspect-ratio reference explains why an automatic dimension matters. If both width and height are explicitly fixed, there is no automatic size for the ratio to calculate. A leftover height rule in a mobile breakpoint can therefore make the ratio appear ineffective.

Separate the constraints in DevTools

Inspect the slot and its image as two boxes. Record computed width, height, minimum size, maximum size and box-sizing. Then look for fixed dimensions inherited from component variants or utility classes. Toggle one constraint at a time so the cause remains visible.

Observed behaviorLikely question to investigate
Ratio changes at one breakpointDoes that breakpoint set an explicit height?
Card grows taller than expectedIs content imposing a minimum size?
Image appears stretchedAre both image dimensions forced without a fitting rule?
Image has empty spaceIs contain preserving a different intrinsic ratio?

Avoid treating the ratio as a hard clipping instruction for text. A card containing copy may need to grow when content expands. If a design requires a fixed media ratio, put that constraint on the media region and let the title and description occupy separate content space.

Choose a consistent media contract

For an asset handoff, record three independent decisions: the slot ratio, the image fit and the focal point if cropped. For example, “16:9 slot, contain, neutral background” is much clearer than “responsive image.” Include the source file’s intrinsic dimensions separately so a later export does not confuse source geometry with layout geometry.

Test a square image, a very wide image and a portrait image inside the same component. Confirm that a missing image still leaves a sensible layout, and check the card at its smallest placement. If the artwork requires a different composition on mobile, plan an alternate source rather than stretching or hiding meaningful information. The responsive delivery guide covers candidate sizes after these layout decisions are settled.
coverAlt: Two 16 by 9 media boxes at widths of 640 and 320 pixels, illustrating proportional heights of 360 and 180 pixels.

title: How to Inspect CSS Pseudo-Elements and Missing Decorations
description: Find styles created by before and after pseudo-elements. Check generated content, box dimensions, positioning and clipping without changing meaningful HTML text.
body:
A small dot, underline or corner decoration may be generated by ::before or ::after rather than a separate HTML element. Inspect the owning element and its pseudo-element rules before searching your assets folder. The decoration’s appearance may come entirely from CSS, including borders, backgrounds and generated content.

Build a decoration with a visible owner

<h2 class="section-title">Project details</h2>
.section-title {
  position: relative;
  padding-inline-start: 1rem;
}
.section-title::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset-inline-start: 0;
  top: 0.2em;
  width: 0.25rem;
  height: 0.8em;
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: currentColor;
}

The heading contains the real text; the pseudo-element draws an accent beside it. The positioned heading supplies the decoration’s containing block. Logical inline positioning lets the accent follow the text direction. This is a small illustration of a CSS technique, not a recreation of a third-party component.

The MDN ::before reference describes generated content and the default inline display. An empty content string is useful for a purely visual shape. If content resolves to none or the rule does not apply, the decoration may never produce a box.

Follow a missing decoration through four checks

  • Select the heading in Elements and inspect its generated pseudo-element when present.
  • Confirm that the selector and content declaration apply at the current breakpoint.
  • Check dimensions, positioning and the actual color against the surface.
  • Inspect clipping and layering on ancestors if the box exists but is not visible.

A width on an ordinary inline box does not behave like a width on an inline-block or positioned box. In the example, absolute positioning makes the dimensions effective. For an inline decorative badge, choose an appropriate display value instead of copying the positioning rules mechanically.

When a mark sits in the wrong corner, inspect the containing block before changing offsets. A missing position rule on the owner can make the decoration align to a more distant ancestor. When a mark disappears only on hover, compare pseudo-element rules for both states rather than assuming the image failed to load.

Keep meaning in the document

Do not put an essential field label, validation error or article heading only into generated content. Assistive technology handling of CSS-generated text can vary, and the content should remain understandable when decorative styles are unavailable. Use real HTML for the information, then add decoration around it.

Record the owner selector, pseudo-element, content value and positioning relationship in your inspection notes. Test a long heading and a right-to-left version if the component supports them. Finally, disable the pseudo-element: the page should lose ornament, not its instructions or meaning. That simple review distinguishes a useful decoration from hidden content debt.
coverAlt: A heading with a blue decorative accent and a separate inspection panel identifying the before pseudo-element.

title: CSS Multiple Backgrounds: Put the Overlay in the Right Layer
description: Build a readable image banner with separate gradient and photo layers. Match background-size and position lists, and avoid shorthand resets during debugging.
body:
In a multiple-background declaration, the first image is painted closest to the viewer. Put a translucent gradient before a photo when the gradient should darken it. If the photo comes first and fully covers the box, it can hide the overlay even though both declarations are valid.

Keep the layer lists aligned

.banner {
  color: white;
  background-color: #17202d;
  background-image:
    linear-gradient(90deg, rgb(0 0 0 / 85%), rgb(0 0 0 / 20%)),
    url("/images/workshop.webp");
  background-size: cover, cover;
  background-position: center, 65% center;
  background-repeat: no-repeat, no-repeat;
  padding: 3rem 1.5rem;
}
.banner-copy { max-width: 32rem; }

Replace the sample path with an asset you have permission to use. The first size and position belong to the gradient; the second pair belongs to the photo. Keeping each list explicit makes the relationship easier to audit. The dark base color provides a surface when the image is missing.

MDN’s multiple backgrounds guide explains paint order and list repetition. A background color belongs beneath the image layers; it is not an additional image that can be moved to the front of the comma-separated list.

Inspect one layer at a time

Temporarily replace the photo with none, then restore it and remove the gradient. This separates an asset-delivery problem from an overlay-order problem. Next, move the banner through its responsive widths and examine where the subject and the text meet. A gradient that works behind a short title may leave the last line of a longer title over a bright part of the photo.

SymptomCheck
Gradient appears absentIs an opaque image listed before it?
Photo repeatsDoes its repeat entry match the photo layer?
Crop moves unexpectedlyCompare the photo’s position entry and box ratio.
Layers vanish in a variantLook for a later background shorthand reset.

A later background shorthand can reset image, size and other related properties you established earlier. When changing only the fallback color in a component variant, use background-color. Inspect the winning declaration before adding more specificity.

Review meaning and contrast separately

Treat decorative background photography differently from an image that carries essential information. If readers need the image to understand a diagram or product detail, use meaningful image markup with a text alternative instead of hiding the information in CSS.

Measure contrast where the text actually lands, using the final image, overlay and responsive layout. The example opacity values are starting points, not a guaranteed contrast result. Test a long headline and the fallback surface with the image blocked. Save the layer order and focal-point decision with the asset so the next image replacement gets the same review.
coverAlt: A diagram of gradient, photo and base-color layers in front-to-back painting order.

title: Respect Reduced Motion Without Hiding Interface Feedback
description: Use prefers-reduced-motion to reduce nonessential movement while keeping clear state changes. Review CSS transitions, JavaScript animation and loading feedback.
body:
Reduced motion should preserve the information a transition communicates while removing unnecessary movement. A panel can appear without sliding across the screen, and a saved state can remain visible without a bouncing confirmation. Start with the usable static state, then add motion only where the user has not requested a reduction.

Enhance a stable button state

.action {
  background: #173f86;
  color: white;
  border: 2px solid transparent;
}
.action:hover { background: #102f65; }
.action:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #2878dd; outline-offset: 3px; }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
  .action { transition: transform 150ms ease; }
  .action:hover { transform: translateY(-2px); }
}

The color change and focus indicator do not depend on animation. The small lift is an optional decoration. This example avoids a hidden initial state: if the media query never matches, the button is still present and usable.

The MDN media-feature reference describes the reduce and no-preference values. The preference concerns motion; it does not instruct you to remove content, stop progress reporting or eliminate every visual distinction between states.

Inventory motion by purpose

MotionReduced-motion alternative
Large panel slideShow the panel immediately.
Decorative parallaxKeep the artwork stationary.
Animated progress illustrationRetain a text status and measured progress if available.
Smooth anchor scrollingUse immediate scrolling.

Review CSS and JavaScript separately. A CSS media query does not automatically stop an animation driven by a canvas library or a timer. For scripted animation, use matchMedia to read the same preference and respond if it changes. Check the animation library’s own configuration rather than layering contradictory overrides on top.

Avoid a blanket rule that forces every duration to an extremely short value without testing behavior. Some applications incorrectly depend on animation-end events to finish a state change. Fix that dependency or preserve the necessary event handling; an accessibility preference should not leave a dialog half-open or a loading control permanently disabled.

Test the whole task with the preference enabled

Enable reduced motion in your operating system or browser emulation, reload, and complete a task from start to finish. Open navigation, submit a sample form, change tabs and follow an anchor. Verify that status messages remain understandable, keyboard focus remains visible and content does not wait for an animation that no longer runs.

Then switch the preference while the page is open if your application supports live changes. Record the expected behavior for each animated component in the handoff. A useful acceptance statement is “the panel opens immediately and focus moves to its first meaningful control,” which can be checked independently of the decorative transition.
coverAlt: A moving button shown with a small lift beside a stationary button that keeps its visible action label.

title: Build a Skip Link That Moves Keyboard Users to the Content
description: Add a visible-on-focus skip link and verify its target, focus behavior and placement above navigation. Test the full keyboard path on real page templates.
body:
A skip link lets a keyboard user bypass repeated navigation and reach the page’s main content. It should be early in the tab order, visible when focused and connected to a real destination. A link that merely changes the URL fragment while leaving the user trapped at the top does not complete that task.

Connect the first link to main content

<a class="skip-link" href="#main-content">Skip to content</a>
<header><!-- Repeated site navigation --></header>
<main id="main-content" tabindex="-1">
  <h1>Project guide</h1>
  <!-- Page-specific content -->
</main>
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: 0.75rem;
  inset-inline-start: 0.75rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  background: white;
  color: #111;
  z-index: 10;
  transform: translateY(-200%);
}
.skip-link:focus { transform: none; }
#main-content { scroll-margin-block-start: 5rem; }

The negative tabindex allows the target to receive focus without adding a permanent extra stop to normal tab navigation. The layer number is only an example: place the link where its ancestor context can appear above your header. Do not use display:none for the unfocused state, because that removes the link from keyboard navigation.

W3C’s skip-link technique describes bypassing repeated material and moving focus beyond it. Keep the wording specific to the destination; “Skip to content” is easier to understand than an unexplained arrow icon.

Test the next Tab, not only the scroll

Reload a page and press Tab from the browser’s page area. Confirm the link appears with readable contrast. Activate it, then press Tab again and inspect where keyboard navigation resumes. It should continue in the main content rather than restarting through the navigation you intended to skip.

Run this sequence on a short page and a long page with a sticky header. Check that the main heading is not hidden behind the header after navigation. If your router intercepts fragment links, verify that it preserves destination and focus behavior. Add focused handling only if your actual application needs it, and test that handling with assistive technology.

Make the pattern survive template changes

Use a unique destination ID on every rendered page and keep it on the actual main region. Duplicate IDs can send navigation to the wrong place. When a page has several repeated regions, consider whether additional bypass links help, but avoid creating a new wall of links before the content.

  • The skip link is reachable before repeated navigation.
  • Its focused state is visible above the header.
  • Activation reaches the correct main region.
  • Subsequent keyboard navigation continues from that region.
  • The behavior survives zoom and a wrapped mobile header.

Include the keyboard sequence in template regression checks. A screenshot of the focused link proves only its appearance; the follow-up Tab test proves whether the shortcut actually saves the user work.
coverAlt: A skip-to-content control above repeated navigation with an arrow leading directly to the main content panel.

title: Native HTML Dialog: A Keyboard and Focus Checklist
description: Build a small modal with the dialog element, showModal and an explicit close action. Check initial focus, Escape, background interaction and focus restoration.
body:
A native dialog opened with showModal provides modal behavior that a positioned div does not acquire from its appearance alone. Start with the native element, give it a clear name and explicit close control, then test the complete keyboard interaction. Styling the backdrop is only one part of a usable modal.

Create a small information dialog

<button type="button" id="open-help">Export help</button>
<dialog id="export-help" aria-labelledby="help-title">
  <h2 id="help-title">Export help</h2>
  <p>Your export includes the selected design notes.</p>
  <form method="dialog">
    <button autofocus>Close help</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
<script>
  const help = document.querySelector("#export-help");
  document.querySelector("#open-help").addEventListener("click", () => {
    help.showModal();
  });
</script>

Place the script after the markup or initialize it after the document is ready. The dialog form closes this informational dialog; it does not send a network request. Autofocus is reasonable for the close button in this tiny example. A larger dialog may need a different initial focus target based on what the user must read or do.

The MDN dialog reference distinguishes modal opening from merely setting the open attribute. With showModal, the dialog enters the top layer and the surrounding document becomes inert. Do not add tabindex to the dialog element itself.

Review the keyboard lifecycle

StepExpected observation
Open using Enter or SpaceThe dialog appears and focus moves inside.
Tab and Shift+TabBackground controls are not available while modal.
Press EscapeThe ordinary informational dialog closes.
Reopen and use Close helpThe explicit close action works.
After either close pathFocus returns to the invoking control when appropriate.

Test both closing routes because application event handlers can alter native behavior. Do not assume clicking the backdrop closes the dialog unless you have explicitly implemented and tested that behavior. The close button gives touch and keyboard users a clear route independent of backdrop behavior.

Keep content usable at a narrow width

dialog {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  width: min(32rem, calc(100% - 2rem));
  max-height: calc(100% - 2rem);
  overflow: auto;
  padding: 1.5rem;
}
dialog::backdrop { background: rgb(0 0 0 / 55%); }

Replace the short paragraph with realistic long content and enlarge the text. The close control must remain reachable. Avoid an unconditional display rule that makes a closed dialog visible; style its layout in a way that preserves the native closed state.

Finally, test the dialog with a screen reader and confirm its name is announced clearly. For a destructive action or a multi-step form, review initial focus, validation and cancellation as separate design decisions. This minimal help dialog demonstrates the lifecycle; it is not a complete interaction specification for every modal workflow.
coverAlt: A labeled help dialog over muted page content, with a highlighted close button and Escape key reminder.

title: Form Labels vs Placeholders: Keep the Field’s Purpose Visible
description: Associate visible labels with form fields, keep examples in helpful text and test repeated components for unique IDs. Build an email field that stays understandable.
body:
A placeholder is a temporary hint inside a field. A label tells the user what the field is for and remains useful after a value is entered. Use a real label as the default, then add instructions or an example where they help. A minimal form should not require users to erase their answer to rediscover the question.

Give the field a stable name and description

<div class="field">
  <label for="contact-email">Email address</label>
  <p id="email-hint">We will send the project reply here.</p>
  <input id="contact-email" name="email" type="email"
    autocomplete="email" aria-describedby="email-hint">
</div>

The for value matches the input ID exactly. The name attribute identifies the submitted form value; it does not replace the label. The description explains use of the address without turning the label into a paragraph. Autocomplete gives the browser a relevant field-purpose hint, while the email type provides native email-entry behavior.

W3C’s labeling controls tutorial covers explicit and implicit associations. Clicking the label should focus its input, which is a useful quick check as well as a practical interaction benefit.

Inspect repeated fields for duplicate IDs

A component can look correct in isolation and fail when rendered twice. If both instances use contact-email, a label or description may resolve to the wrong element. Generate stable unique IDs for repeated instances and update every reference together. Do not solve the collision by removing the label association.

PartJob
Visible labelNames the field’s purpose.
Help textExplains a constraint or use.
PlaceholderOptionally gives a brief example.
Error messageExplains a problem after validation.

Keep those jobs separate in the design file. If a field requires a particular format, put the instruction in persistent help text rather than relying entirely on a placeholder. If the field is optional, make that clear consistently. Do not silently change the label into an error message when validation fails; users still need the original purpose.

Check the filled and enlarged states

Enter a realistic long value, move focus away and inspect the result. The label should remain readable, the help text should still relate clearly to the field, and no floating-label animation should collide with the entered text. Review the same component at increased text size and in the site’s supported themes.

Use the accessibility inspector or a screen reader to verify the field’s accessible name and description. A nearby text node is not proof of a programmatic relationship. Avoid adding an unrelated aria-label that overrides a clear visible label; matching what people see and what assistive technology announces reduces confusion.

Record the label, help copy, optional status and autocomplete purpose in the handoff. Test a second instance of the component before accepting it. Once naming is dependable, the error-message workflow can add validation feedback without replacing the field’s identity.
coverAlt: An email field with a persistent label and separate help text, still visible after an illustrative address is entered.

title: Accessible Form Errors: Connect the Message to the Field
description: Write actionable validation messages and associate them with inputs. Preserve help text, mark invalid fields and test recovery after a failed form submission.
body:
A useful form error identifies the field, explains what needs correction and remains available while the user fixes it. A red border alone does none of those jobs reliably. Keep the field’s label, add a clear text message and connect that message programmatically to the affected control.

Represent an actual validation failure

<label for="project-name">Project name</label>
<p id="project-hint">Use a name your team will recognize.</p>
<input id="project-name" name="projectName"
  aria-invalid="true"
  aria-describedby="project-hint project-error">
<p id="project-error">Enter a project name before continuing.</p>

This markup represents the state after validation has found an empty project name. Do not mark every untouched field invalid when the page first loads. The description references both persistent help and the current error, so validation does not erase the useful instruction.

W3C’s form notification guidance describes associating errors with fields and giving correction advice. The attributes communicate state and relationships; they do not implement validation or replace checks on the server.

Design the recovery path

SituationUseful message
Required field is emptyEnter a project name before continuing.
Upload exceeds a real limitChoose a file smaller than the stated limit.
Server is temporarily unavailableYour changes were not saved. Try again.
A field has an unsupported valueExplain the accepted value or format.

Use limits and accepted formats from the actual product rules. Do not invent a maximum length in the interface that the server does not enforce. Avoid blaming wording such as “You entered invalid data” when a direct instruction explains the remedy more clearly.

For a longer form, provide an error summary with links to the affected fields. Decide whether focus should move to that summary or to the first invalid field after submission, then test the chosen behavior. Dynamically inserted notifications may need an announcement strategy, but announcing every keystroke or duplicating the same message in several live regions can overwhelm users.

Clear stale state without losing work

When the user corrects a field and validation confirms it, remove its invalid state and obsolete error association while retaining any persistent help reference. Preserve the other entered values after a failed submission. A validation system that forces users to retype correct information creates extra work unrelated to the original error.

Test an empty submission, several errors at once, correction of one field and a server-side failure. With a screen reader, inspect the field’s name, invalid state and description. With a keyboard, follow every summary link and confirm that the target is usable. With color removed or changed, check that the error is still understandable.

Record the validation trigger, exact message, field association and recovery behavior in the component specification. That record helps designers and developers review the same interaction rather than comparing only the color of an error border.
coverAlt: A project name field with a visible error message connected to the field, preserving the original label.

title: How to Write Alt Text for UI Screenshots and Icons
description: Choose image alternatives by purpose: informative screenshots, decorative artwork and linked icons. Keep complex instructions in nearby text instead of overloaded alt text.
body:
Write an image alternative for the job the image performs on that page. A screenshot explaining a selected setting needs different text from the same screenshot used as decoration. Begin by asking what the reader would miss if the image were unavailable, then supply that information in the most useful place.

Classify the image before describing it

Image purposeAlternative approach
Screenshot showing a selected settingDescribe the setting or result that matters.
Decorative interface artwork beside equivalent textUse an empty alt attribute.
Image-only linkDescribe the destination or action.
Complex diagram with several stepsProvide a short alternative and full nearby explanation.

The W3C alt decision tree organizes these decisions around context and function. Empty alt and a missing alt attribute are different choices: explicitly mark a decorative image with alt="" instead of leaving its treatment ambiguous.

Make a screenshot support the instruction

<figure>
  <img src="/images/export-settings.webp" width="960" height="600"
    alt="Export settings with SVG selected as the file format.">
  <figcaption>Choose SVG when exporting this vector icon.</figcaption>
</figure>

This is illustrative markup for a screenshot that actually shows that state. The alternative names the relevant selection rather than cataloging every toolbar and pixel. If the article already explains the state completely and the image adds no information, an empty alternative may be more appropriate. Review the whole paragraph and caption together before deciding.

For a screenshot containing an error message, include the important error wording in real article text as well. That makes it searchable, selectable and available without opening the image. Avoid embedding an entire tutorial in one long alt attribute; readers should be able to navigate the instructions as ordinary headings and paragraphs.

Avoid duplicate names inside controls

<a href="/downloads/">
  <img src="/icons/download.svg" alt="" width="20" height="20">
  Download files
</a>

Here the visible link text already names the destination. Repeating “Download files” in the icon’s alternative can make the link name redundant. An image-only link would need an accessible name from the image alternative or another suitable labeling method. Do not substitute a filename such as download-final-v3.svg for a meaningful action.

Review alternatives when the artwork changes

Treat alt text as part of the content record. If a screenshot changes from SVG selected to PNG selected, the alternative must change with it. If an image moves from an explanatory guide to a decorative homepage card, reconsider its purpose rather than copying the old text unchanged.

Read the page with images unavailable and then inspect it with a screen reader. Confirm that the main instructions still work and that decorative images do not create noise. Keep keyword targeting out of this decision: a relevant, accurate alternative helps people understand the page, while a list of search phrases does not describe the image’s purpose.
coverAlt: An illustrative export settings image with SVG selected alongside a concise text description of that meaningful state.

title: Responsive Data Tables Without Losing Row and Column Context
description: Keep data tables readable on narrow screens with semantic headers and a scrollable region. Test keyboard scrolling, long values and relationships between cells.
body:
A data table may need horizontal space to preserve comparisons. On a narrow screen, contain that overflow within a clearly identified region instead of letting the entire page scroll sideways. Keep the table’s header relationships intact so readers can still understand which values belong to which rows and columns.

Keep the data structure in HTML

<div class="table-scroll" role="region"
  aria-label="Export formats" tabindex="0">
  <table>
    <caption>Example asset export choices</caption>
    <thead><tr>
      <th scope="col">Format</th>
      <th scope="col">Typical use</th>
      <th scope="col">Review before export</th>
    </tr></thead>
    <tbody><tr>
      <th scope="row">SVG</th>
      <td>Vector interface icon</td>
      <td>ViewBox and color behavior</td>
    </tr></tbody>
  </table>
</div>
.table-scroll { max-width: 100%; overflow-x: auto; }
.table-scroll:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #246bd1; outline-offset: 3px; }
.table-scroll table { border-collapse: collapse; min-width: 36rem; width: 100%; }
.table-scroll th, .table-scroll td {
  padding: 0.75rem;
  text-align: start;
  border-bottom: 1px solid #bbb;
}

The example minimum width is a design choice to review with real content. It is not an accessibility threshold. The focusable named region gives keyboard users an explicit way to reach the overflow area; verify arrow-key scrolling in the browsers you support.

W3C’s tables tutorial explains header and data-cell relationships. Simple tables can use scope; complex multi-level headers may need more explicit associations. Visual boldness alone does not identify a header programmatically.

Make overflow discoverable

Use a visible cue or a short instruction when the table extends beyond the available area. Do not rely solely on a scrollbar that may be hidden by the operating system. Check that the first column gives enough context while users inspect later columns, and consider a sticky first column only after reviewing its overlap and background behavior.

Avoid reducing text to a tiny size just to force every column onto a phone. Also avoid converting all cells to generic blocks without checking the resulting accessibility tree and reading order. A stacked representation can work, but it must preserve the meaning of each value and should be designed as a deliberate alternate view.

Run a realistic table review

  • Tab into the region and scroll to the last column.
  • Read several cells with a screen reader and confirm their headers.
  • Try long labels, missing values and unusually large numbers.
  • Enlarge text and check that the surrounding page still fits.
  • Confirm that essential columns remain available rather than silently hidden.

For an enormous table, a summary, filters or a separate detail view may help more than additional CSS. Record why a table is needed and which comparisons users must make. Then evaluate the mobile treatment against those tasks, not only against a screenshot of the first row.
coverAlt: A narrow scrollable region containing a wider data table with visible column headers and a horizontal scroll indicator.

title: Wrap Long URLs and Filenames with CSS overflow-wrap
description: Stop long strings from breaking cards while preserving readable text. Compare anywhere, break-word, nowrap and deliberate truncation with a filename example.
