keyword: css wrap long words overflow wrap
body:
A long filename, URL or identifier can overflow a component even when ordinary sentences fit. Use overflow-wrap when an otherwise unbreakable string needs an emergency line break. First make sure wrapping is allowed and the containing box can shrink; a text rule cannot repair every fixed-width layout constraint.

Build a filename row that can shrink

<div class="file-row">
  <span aria-hidden="true">↳</span>
  <span class="file-name">homepage-navigation-component-review-notes.txt</span>
</div>
.file-row { display: flex; gap: 0.5rem; max-width: 100%; }
.file-name {
  min-width: 0;
  white-space: normal;
  overflow-wrap: anywhere;
}

The filename stays complete in the document and can wrap inside the available row. The min-width rule addresses the flex item’s sizing constraint, while overflow-wrap addresses the string itself. Test the real component’s ancestors too: an explicit wide width farther up the tree can still make the page overflow.

MDN’s overflow-wrap reference distinguishes anywhere from break-word. Both can break a long string, but the new break opportunities affect min-content sizing for anywhere and not for break-word. That distinction can matter in intrinsic grid and flex sizing.

Choose a text policy, not a global patch

ContentStarting policy
Long filename or visible URLAllow wrapping with an emergency break.
Ordinary prosePreserve normal word boundaries.
Code where line structure mattersUse a contained scrolling code block.
Compact list with a detail viewConsider deliberate truncation with full text available.

Do not apply word-break:break-all to every paragraph just because one identifier is too long. It can split ordinary words aggressively and make reading harder. If you use hyphenation for prose, check the document language and the actual language-specific behavior; it is a different decision from wrapping an arbitrary URL.

If nothing wraps, inspect white-space on the element and its ancestors. A nowrap declaration can defeat the intended presentation. Then inspect the flex or grid item’s minimum size and the component’s explicit width. Keep these checks separate so you do not accumulate unrelated fixes.

Review truncation as a product decision

An ellipsis can be useful when users can easily open a full-detail view, but it may hide the exact part of a filename they need to distinguish. A hover-only title tooltip is not a dependable substitute for accessible full text on touch and keyboard devices. Decide where the complete value can be read and copied.

Test a short name, a long unbroken identifier, a URL with query parameters and text in another supported language. Copy the displayed value and confirm you did not insert literal spaces or hyphens into the data merely to influence layout. Save the chosen wrapping policy with the component so future content does not recreate the same overflow bug.
coverAlt: A long filename wrapping over three lines inside a narrow component without changing the underlying text.

title: Variable Font Axes: Match the File to Your CSS
description: Use a variable font’s real weight range and supported axes. Prefer standard CSS properties for common axes and verify the rendered face before tuning typography.
body:
A variable font can contain a range of designs in one file, but the available axes depend on that file. Do not assume every variable font supports width, slant or optical size. Start with the font’s own axis information, then map the design choices you need into CSS.

Declare the range the file actually contains

@font-face {
  font-family: "Project Variable";
  src: url("/fonts/project-variable.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 300 800;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}
.article-title {
  font-family: "Project Variable", system-ui, sans-serif;
  font-weight: 650;
}

This example assumes a real upright variable file with a 300–800 weight range. Replace the name, URL and range with your licensed font’s values. A static regular font does not gain variable weights just because the descriptor declares a range.

MDN’s variable fonts guide describes registered and custom axes. Prefer a high-level property such as font-weight for its corresponding common axis. Use font-variation-settings deliberately for axes that need it rather than combining several competing controls for the same weight.

Create a small axis specimen

SpecimenWhat to compare
Same heading at 400, 550 and 700Stroke weight, wrapping and hierarchy.
Body copy with supported optical sizingSmall-text shapes and reading comfort.
Long navigation labelWidth and space constraints.
Accented characters and symbolsWhether the intended font supplies the glyphs.

Keep the specimen text and size constant while changing one axis. Otherwise, a different line break may come from the font size or container width rather than the axis you are evaluating. Compare actual rendered text instead of relying on an axis slider’s numeric value as evidence of visual quality.

For optical sizing, font-optical-sizing:auto is meaningful when the selected face supports an optical-size axis. Custom axis tags and ranges should come from the font documentation. Copying an unfamiliar four-letter setting from another site may have no effect on your chosen face.

Verify the selected face and the handoff

Inspect rendered fonts in DevTools and confirm that the variable file is actually used. If a heading falls back to a system font, adjusting variation settings will not solve the delivery problem. If one style differs, compare the face’s declared style and range with the requested CSS before changing the overall typography system.

Record the font filename, supported axes, ranges and selected role values in your design notes. Keep a separate record for any italic file. Measure the real downloaded bytes for the faces your site needs before making performance claims; one variable file is not automatically smaller than every possible static-font setup.

Finally, review paragraph density, buttons and long headings at narrow widths. A visually attractive weight in a specimen is only a candidate until it works in the components that use it.
coverAlt: A weight-axis specimen showing three example settings, 400, 500 and 700, along a supported range.

title: When to Preload a Web Font—and How to Verify It Helps
description: Preload a genuinely critical font with matching request settings. Check for duplicate downloads, unused hints and competition with other early page resources.
body:
Preload a font when it is needed early and normal discovery starts its request too late. Do not preload every font in the project. A hint spends bandwidth earlier; it is useful only if that earlier work helps the current page rather than competing with more important resources.

Match the hint to the actual face

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/interface-regular.woff2"
  as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
@font-face {
  font-family: "Interface";
  src: url("/fonts/interface-regular.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 400;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}

The example assumes this regular face appears in the initial viewport. Both references point to the same file. The preload starts a fetch; the font-face rule and the text’s font-family still determine how the font is used. Keep the file’s actual weight and style descriptors accurate.

The MDN preload reference explains the request-matching role of as, type and crossorigin. Font requests use CORS behavior, so the crossorigin attribute matters even when the font URL is on the same origin.

Record a baseline before adding hints

Open the page with DevTools, disable cache for the controlled test and use the same network profile for both versions. Record when the font request begins, whether text is visible during loading and which face is actually rendered. Also note the major image and stylesheet requests that share the early loading period.

Before/after checkWhy it matters
Font request starts earlierShows whether discovery changed.
Only the intended file is requestedAvoids mismatched or duplicate work.
Font is used by initial contentAvoids wasting an early hint.
Important image timing remains acceptableChecks competition for bandwidth.
Warm navigation still worksCovers ordinary repeat visits.

Do not claim a speed improvement from request order alone. Compare the visible result and repeat the measurement under consistent conditions. A small timing difference from one run can be noise. Keep your findings specific to the page and device conditions tested.

Remove hints that no longer fit the page

A global header can preload a display font on pages that never use it. A redesign can change the hero from bold to regular while leaving the old hint behind. Review preloads when typography roles or page templates change. Browser warnings about unused preloads are evidence to investigate, not instructions to add more hints.

For a variable font or language subset, verify which exact file the browser selects for the initial text. Avoid preloading every possible subset “just in case.” Keep fallback and font-display behavior as separate decisions; fetching a face earlier does not guarantee that layout will remain stable when its metrics replace the fallback.

Document the page, face, reason for the hint and the before/after observation. That small record makes it easier to remove a preload later if its original benefit disappears.
coverAlt: Two schematic resource-discovery timelines comparing a later font request with an earlier preload, without measured timing claims.

title: CSS Print Styles: Make Guides Readable on Paper and PDF
description: Create a focused print stylesheet for article pages. Remove repeated chrome, preserve meaningful content and inspect page breaks, code blocks and table overflow.
body:
A page designed for a screen can waste paper or hide information when printed. Build a print view around the content someone wants to keep: title, explanation, examples and references. Remove repeated navigation where appropriate, but preserve content that the reader needs after the browser is gone.

Start with explicit print overrides

@media print {
  .site-nav, .newsletter-form, .floating-toolbar { display: none; }
  body { color: #000; background: #fff; }
  main { width: auto; max-width: none; margin: 0; }
  .sticky-summary { position: static; }
  pre { white-space: pre-wrap; overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
  h2, h3 { break-after: avoid; }
  figure { break-inside: avoid; }
}
@page { margin: 18mm; }

Use selectors that exist in your project. The margin is an example to preview with your expected paper sizes. Avoid a universal rule that prevents every element from breaking across pages; a large section still needs to flow, and an image taller than a page cannot remain intact simply because CSS asks it to.

MDN’s printing guide explains print media styles and page rules. Normal cascade precedence still applies, so check which declaration wins when a screen rule seems to survive your print stylesheet.

Keep the useful information visible

Open every disclosure or alternate tab that contains essential printable content, or provide a deliberate print representation of that information. Do not assume a closed panel will be printed just because its data exists somewhere in the application. Test the output rather than relying on the screen DOM alone.

Inspect tables and code blocks carefully. A scrollable region can hide offscreen content in print. A wide comparison table may need a simpler print layout or a dedicated export. Wrapping code can help, but check that long lines and indentation remain understandable. Never silently drop columns that are required to interpret a result.

Use print preview as the acceptance check

Preview itemQuestion
First pageAre title and context present?
Page boundariesAre headings stranded without their following text?
FiguresAre meaningful labels readable?
Tables and codeIs any content clipped off the paper?
LinksCan the printed reader identify important references?

If you append URLs to printed links, target references deliberately. A global a::after rule can print navigation fragments, long query strings and duplicate addresses everywhere. For a technical guide, a short source list may be easier to read than expanding every inline link.

Preview both Letter and A4 if your audience uses both. Check with background graphics disabled, because print settings may omit them. A white label on a background that disappears can become unreadable. Save a PDF from the actual browser print flow and inspect its last page as well as its first. Media emulation is useful during development, but pagination needs its own review.
coverAlt: An article screen with navigation beside a simplified print page retaining the title, text and figure.

title: Style Link Underlines Without Losing Readability
description: Tune underline offset and thickness for inline links. Test wrapped text, descenders and focus states while preserving a clear visual cue beyond link color.
body:
An underline helps readers distinguish an inline link from surrounding prose without relying only on color. Adjust its thickness and distance from the text to suit the typeface, then test a link that wraps. A decorative border or background trick may look good on one line and fail when the text spans two.

Use native text decoration first

.article-copy a {
  color: #174fa0;
  text-decoration-line: underline;
  text-decoration-thickness: 0.08em;
  text-underline-offset: 0.18em;
  text-decoration-skip-ink: auto;
}
.article-copy a:hover { text-decoration-thickness: 0.14em; }
.article-copy a:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

The em values scale with the text size. They are specimen values to evaluate with your actual font, not universal ideal settings. The underline remains present before hover, and keyboard focus has its own visible treatment.

MDN’s underline-offset reference explains that offset is separate from the text-decoration shorthand and affects underlines rather than every decoration type. Set it explicitly when your design depends on a particular distance.

Build a specimen that exposes weak spots

Use a sentence containing letters with descenders, such as “Review typography and spacing,” and make the link long enough to wrap at a narrow width. Compare regular and bold linked text. Inspect whether the underline crowds the next line, disappears around too many glyphs or looks disconnected from its text.

SpecimenReview goal
Short link in body copyClearly identifiable before interaction.
Two-line linkDecoration follows both line fragments.
Link with g, p, q and yDescenders remain readable.
Focused linkKeyboard location is unambiguous.
Link on a colored surfaceText and focus treatment remain visible.

Avoid adding padding that unexpectedly changes the line box just to move an underline. Use the underline properties for the decoration itself. If you need a custom animated treatment, compare it with the native baseline under wrapping, zoom and reduced motion before replacing the simpler approach.

Keep link purpose clear in the words

A refined underline cannot rescue vague link text. “Read the font-loading checklist” communicates more than several identical “Learn more” links scattered through a guide. Keep the label useful in its surrounding sentence and make the destination predictable.

Review hover, focus and visited styling in the page’s supported themes. Do not remove outlines without an equivalent focus indication. Use the contrast workflow for the actual text and surface combinations instead of assuming blue always passes.

Save the chosen values as part of the body-link style, distinct from navigation buttons or card links. A single global link rule can accidentally underline logos or disrupt a button treatment. Scope the typography decision to the places where readers benefit from an inline text cue.
coverAlt: A two-line inline link with underlines that follow both text lines and leave room around the letters.

title: Keep Anchor Headings Visible Below a Sticky Header
description: Fix headings hidden after anchor navigation with scroll margins or container padding. Test direct fragment URLs, changing header heights and keyboard navigation.
body:
An anchor can scroll to the correct heading while a sticky header covers it. Reserve space for the target during scrolling instead of adding blank spacer elements to every section. Start by measuring the header in the state where the anchor lands, including any notice bar above it.

Apply an offset to the targets

<nav aria-label="On this page">
  <a href="#export-options">Export options</a>
</nav>
<h2 id="export-options">Export options</h2>
:root { --header-clearance: 5.5rem; }
.article h2[id], .article h3[id] {
  scroll-margin-top: var(--header-clearance);
}
@media (max-width: 40rem) {
  :root { --header-clearance: 7rem; }
}

Place the example heading inside the article container. The offsets are sample values; measure your own desktop and mobile header rather than copying them blindly. The margin affects scrolling alignment, not the ordinary gap between the heading and the preceding paragraph.

The MDN scroll-margin-top reference defines the target’s scroll-area outset. If the same clearance should apply broadly within one scrolling container, scroll-padding-top on that container is another design option. Avoid unintentionally applying both and creating a much larger gap.

Identify the element that actually scrolls

A documentation layout may scroll the page, a central content pane or a dialog body. Put the offset strategy on the relevant targets or scrolling container. Changing the root element will not necessarily solve an anchor inside a separately scrolling pane.

Test routeWhat to inspect
Click a table-of-contents linkHeading appears below the header.
Load a URL with its fragmentInitial landing is also readable.
Use browser Back after another anchorNavigation returns to the expected section.
Follow a link near the page endLimited remaining scroll space is handled sensibly.
Enlarge text until the header wrapsClearance still matches the header.

If the header height changes after loading, a fixed offset can become stale. Prefer a layout with predictable header dimensions where practical. If the application measures a dynamic header, update one shared clearance value and test it when banners appear or disappear. Do not scatter slightly different offsets across section stylesheets.

Separate scrolling from focus and motion

Scrolling a heading into view does not by itself complete a keyboard focus-management strategy. Test the next keyboard action after navigation, especially for a skip link or client-side route change. Keep the destination ID unique and stable so bookmarks remain meaningful.

If you enable smooth scrolling, provide an immediate-scrolling path for reduced-motion users. Review direct fragment navigation after fonts and images load as well: layout shifts can move a heading even when its initial offset was correct. The acceptance condition is a visible destination with a sensible continuation of navigation, not merely a changed hash in the address bar.
coverAlt: A sticky header with a visible clearance gap above the anchor heading, illustrating scroll-margin-top.

title: Use currentColor to Keep SVG Icons in Sync with Text
description: Make inline SVG icons inherit a component’s color through fill or stroke. Diagnose fixed colors, external image boundaries and accidental changes to multicolor artwork.
body:
Use currentColor in an inline SVG when an icon should follow its surrounding text color. A button can then change text and icon together on hover or in another theme. First determine whether the drawing uses filled shapes, strokes or both; replacing every color indiscriminately can destroy the artwork.

Build a stroke icon inside a labeled button

<button class="download" type="button">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="20" height="20"
    fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"
    stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"
    aria-hidden="true" focusable="false">
    <path d="M12 3v12m-4-4 4 4 4-4M5 17v4h14v-4" />
  </svg>
  Download sample
</button>
.download { color: #174fa0; }
.download:hover { color: #102f65; }

The path is an original simple download illustration. The visible text names the button, so the decorative SVG is hidden from assistive technology. Connect the button to the actual application action separately; the example only demonstrates the color relationship.

MDN’s SVG color reference explains that color supplies currentColor indirectly. Setting color alone does not paint a shape: fill or stroke must use the value. A filled icon might use fill="currentColor" instead of the stroke-based setup above.

Inspect the source of a stubborn color

ObservationNext check
Stroke changes but center does notLook for a separate fixed fill.
One path stays blackInspect that path’s own attributes or CSS.
Every icon ignores the button colorCheck whether a descendant explicitly sets color.
SVG in an img ignores page colorThe external image is a separate styling boundary.

An SVG loaded through an img element does not inherit the surrounding page’s color the same way inline markup does. Choose an appropriate delivery method rather than trying increasingly specific selectors that cannot reach inside the image. A CSS mask can be useful for a monochrome shape; inline SVG provides direct control over its parts.

Do not replace intentional none values with currentColor. A stroke icon often depends on an unfilled interior. Likewise, a multicolor logo may need its original palette and should not be treated as a monochrome interface symbol. Review brand artwork separately from action icons.

Validate the component in context

Check the icon and text on light and dark surfaces, in hover and focus states, and when the button is disabled. If the surrounding component uses opacity, review the combined result rather than assuming the inherited color remains readable. Compare the icon at its actual small display size so thin strokes are not judged only in an enlarged preview.

Record whether the asset is filled or stroked, its viewBox, intended size and color policy in the asset handoff. For an icon-only control, add a clear accessible name to the control. Keeping color inheritance and labeling as explicit decisions makes a reusable icon easier to maintain across themes and interaction states.
coverAlt: Two download buttons in different colors whose inline stroke icons match the button text through currentColor.

title: Why Flexbox Shrinks Your Button—and How to Fix It
description: Diagnose a squeezed button in a flex row. Inspect the flex basis, minimum size and available space, then decide which item should shrink or wrap.
body:
A width on a flex item is not always its final width. When a row runs out of space, shrinkable items can become narrower. For a file row with a filename and an action button, give the text room to adapt while protecting the action’s readable label. If neither fits, change the arrangement rather than hiding the overflow.

Give each item an explicit job

<div class="file-row">
  <span class="file-name">homepage-navigation-review.txt</span>
  <button class="file-action" type="button">View details</button>
</div>
.file-row { display: flex; gap: 1rem; align-items: center; }
.file-name { flex: 1 1 auto; min-inline-size: 0; overflow-wrap: anywhere; }
.file-action { flex: 0 0 auto; }
@media (max-width: 28rem) {
  .file-row { flex-direction: column; align-items: stretch; }
}

This example lets the filename wrap and moves to a vertical layout at a deliberately chosen breakpoint. The button is a layout specimen; connect its action in your application. Do not copy the breakpoint without checking your actual labels, font and container width.

Check the shrink calculation before changing width

The browser distributes negative free space using each item’s shrink factor multiplied by its flex base size. Equal shrink factors therefore do not imply equal pixel reductions. Minimum-size constraints can also stop an item shrinking. In DevTools, inspect flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis and the computed minimum width together.

Reference: MDN: flex-shrink.

Temporarily remove a fixed width on the row to see whether the problem comes from its parent. Then disable the button’s shrink factor. If the button recovers but the row overflows, the experiment has located the tradeoff; it has not completed the repair. Decide how the filename and row should respond at that size.

Review realistic content

  • Try a short filename, a long unbroken filename and a translated action label.
  • Zoom the page and check that the action remains visible without horizontal page scrolling.
  • Keep the focus outline clear of clipping ancestors and neighboring text.
  • Check the vertical layout with two actions if your real component supports them.

Record the flexible item, protected item and layout-change condition in the component handoff. Avoid adding flex-shrink: 0 to every child: a row full of nonshrinking items simply moves the shortage outside the container. The final design should explain where the extra content goes.
coverAlt: A flexible filename beside a protected View details button, with a second row showing the stacked narrow-screen arrangement.

title: CSS Grid auto-fit vs auto-fill: What Happens to Empty Tracks?
description: Compare auto-fit and auto-fill with a sparse card grid. Understand empty tracks, minimum card widths and why the two values can look identical.
keyword: css grid auto fit vs auto fill
body:
Use auto-fit when a sparse set of cards should expand into available space. Use auto-fill when you want empty repeated tracks to remain part of the grid. The difference becomes visible when there is room for more columns than the content occupies; a full grid can make both declarations look the same.

Compare the same three cards

.card-grid {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  grid-template-columns:
    repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1fr));
}
/* Compare by changing only auto-fit to auto-fill. */

Start with three cards in a container wide enough for four minimum-width tracks. Keep the content and gap constant while switching the keyword. With auto-fit, empty repeated tracks collapse after placement. With auto-fill, those tracks remain. The 1fr maximum distributes free space across the tracks that remain.

Reference: MDN: repeat() and empty tracks.

Avoid confusing an empty cell with an empty track

A gap at the end of the last row does not necessarily represent an empty column. If earlier rows already occupy that column, the track is not empty. Test one card, three cards and enough cards for several rows. This separates the sparse-grid behavior from ordinary row wrapping.

The nested min() keeps the minimum from exceeding the available inline space when the container is narrower than 15rem. It does not make every kind of child content shrink: a fixed-width image or long unbroken value can still overflow. Inspect those children if the outer grid is correctly sized.

Choose using a content scenario

Imagine a saved-project screen with only one project. A card that expands across the full content area may feel oversized, even though auto-fit is behaving correctly. You could constrain the whole grid’s maximum width or choose auto-fill to retain the intended track structure. On a comparison strip with two equally important options, expansion may be exactly what you want.

  • Measure at the component’s actual width, not only the browser width.
  • Inspect the grid overlay to see track boundaries.
  • Check image crops and text wrapping after a card expands.
  • Verify that the one-item layout still has an obvious reading order.

Save screenshots with the item count and container width in the handoff. Those two facts explain the behavior more clearly than a screenshot of a fully populated grid alone.
coverAlt: Three cards expand across an auto-fit row, while an auto-fill row keeps an empty fourth track.

title: svh, dvh and lvh: Choose a Mobile Viewport Height
description: Choose a viewport-height unit for mobile sections. Compare stable small viewports with dynamic sizing and test browser bars, long content and keyboards.
body:
For a mobile introduction that should fit while browser controls are visible, start with a minimum height based on svh. For a surface that should resize as those controls expand or retract, consider dvh. Use lvh only when sizing against the largest viewport is intentional. The right unit depends on whether stability or filling the changing visible area matters more.

Make a landing section a minimum, not a ceiling

.intro {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  min-block-size: 100vh;
  min-block-size: 100svh;
  padding: 2rem 1.25rem;
  display: grid;
  align-content: center;
}

In a normal horizontal writing mode, this gives the section a viewport-height minimum while allowing long content to make it taller. The earlier vh declaration is a fallback. Do not turn it into a fixed height plus hidden overflow: enlarged text and additional copy must still have somewhere to go.

Reference: MDN: viewport-relative length units.

Separate three sizing goals

  • svh uses the small viewport and stays stable as browser controls retract.
  • lvh uses the large viewport; browser controls may cover content when expanded.
  • dvh follows the dynamic viewport and can change the layout during scrolling.

For a project preview, a stable introduction may be preferable to an area that grows and shrinks around its headline. For an application shell, dynamic sizing may be useful, but its scroll regions and focus behavior need a separate review. The unit by itself does not design those interactions.

Test the events that desktop resizing misses

On a real mobile browser, load the page with controls expanded, scroll until they retract, then reverse direction. Rotate the device and zoom text where supported. Focus a field near the bottom and open the on-screen keyboard. Keyboard resizing policies differ, so do not assume dvh guarantees that a focused field or submit button remains visible.

Use a tall sample paragraph and the longest expected heading. Record whether the section grows naturally, whether any nested scroll area becomes difficult to reach, and whether the page jumps during browser-bar transitions. A desktop device frame is useful for width checks but cannot establish all of this behavior.

If a sticky header shares the screen, decide whether the section includes the header or sits below it. Subtract a header height only when that height is actually controlled; a wrapped navigation bar can invalidate a hardcoded subtraction.
coverAlt: Three mobile outlines compare small, dynamic and large viewport sizing with browser-control areas shown above the content.

title: CSS calc(): Build Gutters Without Guessing Pixel Widths
description: Use calc() to combine relative widths and fixed gutters. Check arithmetic syntax, box sizing and the containing block with a small layout example.
body:
Use calc() when a CSS value genuinely needs arithmetic, such as a container width minus two gutters. Keep the formula connected to a clear design rule. A calculation that compensates for several unrelated offsets becomes difficult to maintain when a font, breakpoint or parent layout changes.

Express a page container rule

.page-container {
  --gutter: 1.25rem;
  box-sizing: border-box;
  inline-size: calc(100% - 2 * var(--gutter));
  max-inline-size: 72rem;
  margin-inline: auto;
}

The percentage refers to the available containing-block width, while the rem gutter follows the root font size. At a 16px root size, the two illustrative gutters total 40px. A 400px containing block therefore gives the container a 360px width before its maximum becomes relevant. Change the root size and the result should change deliberately.

Reference: MDN: calc() syntax and value types.

Find the invalid part of a formula

Put whitespace around addition and subtraction operators. Keep units inside the expression, and ensure the result is valid for the property. For example, calc(100% - 2rem) is a length-percentage expression; calc(100 - 2) produces a number and is not an ordinary width. Inspect a crossed-out declaration before trying to fix its visual result elsewhere.

/* Valid: a length divided by a number */
.tile { inline-size: calc((100% - 1rem) / 2); }

This second expression describes two equal tiles separated by one 1rem gap, but Grid is usually clearer for the complete layout. Use the formula to understand the arithmetic; do not duplicate it across every tile if a two-column grid can own the relationship centrally.

Review the box around the calculation

If the result still overflows, inspect padding, borders and box-sizing. A content-box width plus horizontal padding can exceed the space you calculated. Also check that 100% is based on the parent you intended. A nested container calculates from its own context, not automatically from the browser window.

  • Resize the containing block through the minimum and maximum design widths.
  • Increase text size to check that rem-based gutters remain sensible.
  • Remove one declaration at a time when diagnosing doubled spacing.
  • Document whether the container or its parent owns the side inset.

A useful handoff includes the rule in words: “centered, capped at 72rem, with equal 1.25rem side clearance.” That makes the formula reviewable without requiring someone to reverse-engineer a screenshot.
coverAlt: A centered container with two equal side gutters and the formula 100 percent minus twice the gutter.

title: Why a Fixed or Absolute Element Moves with Its Parent
description: Trace the containing block of an absolute or fixed element. Reproduce transformed-ancestor behavior and choose where the positioned component belongs.
keyword: fixed position transformed parent containing block
body:
When a fixed control scrolls with a section, inspect the section’s ancestors before changing its offsets. A transformed ancestor can establish the containing block for a fixed descendant. Absolute positioning also depends on a containing block, so top: 0 is only meaningful once you know which box supplies that origin.

Reproduce the boundary

<section class="preview">
  <p>Preview content</p>
  <button class="help" type="button">Help</button>
</section>
.preview {
  min-height: 60rem;
  transform: translateX(0);
}
.help { position: fixed; right: 1rem; bottom: 1rem; }

Although translateX(0) creates no visible movement, its computed transform is not none. The help control is positioned against the transformed ancestor rather than behaving as a simple viewport-fixed control. Temporarily disable transform and compare while scrolling. Keep the rest of the page unchanged so the experiment has one variable.

Reference: MDN: identifying a containing block.

Trace the ancestor chain

For an absolute child, start with the nearest ancestor whose position is not static, then check other containing-block creators. For a fixed child, look for transforms and related properties such as containment that alter the normal viewport relationship. The MDN reference lists these cases; inspect computed styles because the relevant rule may come from a utility class.

A z-index change answers a layering question, not a coordinate-system question. If the control is visible but attached to the wrong area, increasing its layer will not make it follow the viewport. Likewise, removing overflow may expose the control without changing the box its offsets use.

Choose the component’s owner

If Help belongs to the whole application, placing it outside the transformed preview can make the intended relationship explicit. If it belongs only to that preview, absolute positioning inside a deliberately positioned wrapper may be more appropriate. Moving markup can change inherited styles and event handling, so review those effects as part of the repair.

  • Scroll the page and any nested scroller separately.
  • Run the animation that originally required the transform.
  • Check focus visibility near the edges of the preview.
  • Resize the layout and confirm the control does not cover important content.

In the handoff, name the element that owns the coordinate system. “Bottom right of the preview panel” and “bottom right of the viewport” are different requirements, even when they happen to align in one screenshot.
coverAlt: A fixed help control inside a transformed preview panel, illustrating that its positioning boundary belongs to the ancestor.

title: Build a Scroll-Snap Gallery That Still Scrolls Naturally
description: Create a horizontal card gallery with CSS scroll snap. Set the container and item roles, preserve keyboard access and choose proximity snapping deliberately.
body:
CSS scroll snap can help a horizontal gallery settle near a card edge without replacing native scrolling. Put the snap policy on the scroll container and the alignment on its children. Start with proximity snapping for a reading-oriented gallery, then test whether stronger snapping actually helps the task.

Use a named scroll region

<section aria-labelledby="samples-title">
  <h2 id="samples-title">Layout samples</h2>
  <div class="samples" tabindex="0" role="region"
       aria-label="Scrollable layout samples">
    <article class="sample"><h3>Editorial</h3><p>Sample notes.</p></article>
    <article class="sample"><h3>Catalog</h3><p>Sample notes.</p></article>
    <article class="sample"><h3>Dashboard</h3><p>Sample notes.</p></article>
  </div>
</section>
.samples {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1rem;
  overflow-x: auto;
  scroll-snap-type: x proximity;
  scroll-padding-inline: 1rem;
  padding: 1rem;
}
.sample { flex: 0 0 min(85%, 22rem); scroll-snap-align: start; }
.samples:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #174fa0; outline-offset: 2px; }

The next card can peek into view, providing a cue that more content is available. Keep a scrollbar or another clear cue rather than assuming users will discover a horizontal gesture. The focusable region supports keyboard testing; avoid unnecessary extra tab stops in galleries that already have a better keyboard interaction model.

Reference: MDN: scroll-snap-type.

Check both the container and its children

If nothing snaps, confirm that the region actually overflows and that the children have snap alignment. A flex row whose cards shrink to fit may never become scrollable. If it feels too aggressive, compare proximity with mandatory using long cards and a small viewport. Snapping should not make content hard to inspect between preferred positions.

Review the whole interaction

Tab into the region, use the available keyboard scrolling controls, then Tab onward. Check that focus remains visible and that links inside later cards can be reached. Try touch, trackpad and a mouse with horizontal scrolling. Increase text size so each card becomes taller and review whether the surrounding page still scrolls comfortably.

Do not automatically add looping, autoplay or smooth scripted movement. Those are separate product decisions with additional controls and motion considerations. For a simple set of examples, native scrolling plus a clear alignment policy may be enough. Record the card width, gap, snap alignment and input methods checked in the handoff.
coverAlt: A horizontally scrolling sample gallery with the next card partially visible and a marked start alignment.

title: Use details and summary for Simple Disclosure Panels
description: Build a native disclosure with details and summary. Style its open state, avoid Boolean-attribute mistakes and review labels, focus and essential content.
body:
Use details and summary when someone should be able to reveal a small piece of supporting information in place. The browser provides the basic open-and-close interaction. This is a useful starting point for export notes or optional explanations, provided the summary clearly describes what will be revealed.

Start with native markup

<details class="export-note">
  <summary>What is included in this sample export?</summary>
  <p>The sample includes spacing labels and color values.
     It does not include source images.</p>
</details>
.export-note { border: 1px solid #b7beca; border-radius: .75rem; }
.export-note summary { padding: 1rem; cursor: pointer; }
.export-note p { padding-inline: 1rem; }
.export-note[open] { background: #f3f6fb; }
.export-note summary:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #174fa0;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

The sample export is hypothetical content, not a statement about a specific product’s output. Replace it with the actual information your interface needs. Keep summary as the first child and preserve its native affordance unless you provide an equally understandable replacement.

Reference: MDN: details element.

Understand the open attribute

open is Boolean: its presence opens the panel. Writing open="false" still leaves it open. To close it in markup, remove the attribute. If scripting is needed, set the element’s open property to false rather than treating the string “false” as a closed state.

A shared name can group disclosures so opening one closes another in supporting browsers. Choose that behavior intentionally. Keeping several panels open may help readers compare answers; closing a previous answer automatically can interrupt that task. Test the grouped behavior against your browser requirements before depending on it.

Review content and interaction

  • Use a meaningful summary instead of repeated “More” labels.
  • Tab to the summary and toggle the panel with the keyboard.
  • Check that the focus indicator survives the rounded container styling.
  • Read the open and closed state with the assistive technologies you support.

Do not place the only explanation of a critical error inside a closed panel. A disclosure is best for supplementary detail, not information someone must notice to finish a form. Also avoid nesting unrelated action buttons inside the summary; they create competing interactions in the same target.

For handoff, capture both states and specify the default. Review a long summary at a narrow width: the text should wrap without colliding with the marker, and the expanded body should remain readable without a fixed-height crop.
coverAlt: A closed disclosure summary above an open disclosure with visible supporting text and a downward marker.

title: Review Accessible Tabs with Manual Activation
description: Audit a manual-activation tab interface. Separate keyboard focus from selection and check tab roles, panel relationships, arrow keys and content access.
body:
In manually activated tabs, arrow keys move between tab labels while Enter or Space selects a tab and reveals its panel. Focus and selection are separate states. This is useful when switching panels is expensive or delayed, because exploring the labels does not need to start every panel transition.

Write down the state model

<div role="tablist" aria-label="Project information">
  <button id="tab-overview" role="tab" aria-selected="true"
    aria-controls="panel-overview" tabindex="0">Overview</button>
  <button id="tab-files" role="tab" aria-selected="false"
    aria-controls="panel-files" tabindex="-1">Files</button>
</div>
<section id="panel-overview" role="tabpanel"
  aria-labelledby="tab-overview" tabindex="0">Project overview.</section>
<section id="panel-files" role="tabpanel"
  aria-labelledby="tab-files" tabindex="0" hidden>Project files.</section>

This markup is a state specimen for review, not a complete tabs implementation. It needs keyboard and activation logic. Do not ship the roles alone and assume native buttons provide arrow-key navigation. These example panels start with plain text, so they are focusable; a panel beginning with an appropriate focusable element can use a different entry strategy.

Reference: WAI-ARIA APG: tabs pattern.

Run a keyboard sequence

  • Tab into the widget: focus should arrive on its active tab.
  • Press Right Arrow: focus moves to the next label without changing the displayed panel.
  • Press Enter or Space: selection moves, the old panel hides and the new one appears.
  • Press Tab: leave the tab list and reach the active panel or its meaningful first control.
  • Check wraparound at the first and last tabs; test Home and End if provided.

For a horizontal tab list, do not capture Up and Down simply because the script already handles other arrows. Those keys normally remain available for page scrolling. Review vertical tabs against their corresponding keyboard model instead of copying a horizontal handler unchanged.

Inspect what changes on activation

Compare aria-selected, tabindex, hidden panels and the visible selection indicator before and after the action. The selected tab must reference the correct panel, and that panel must reference its label. A focus ring should remain distinguishable from the selected-state treatment; a screenshot where both look identical can hide an interaction bug.

Use two deliberately different panel contents during testing, such as a short overview and a long file list. Confirm that hidden controls cannot receive focus, repeated IDs do not appear when a second widget is added, and loading states do not leave selection pointing at stale content. For production code, start from a reviewed implementation and test it with your actual content and supported assistive technologies.
coverAlt: Overview remains selected while a focus ring highlights Files, with Enter shown as the activation step.

title: Build a Small Help Panel with the HTML Popover API
description: Use a native popover for optional help. Connect its button, provide a close action and check dismissal, keyboard navigation and non-modal behavior.
body:
A native popover can show optional help above page content without turning the whole page into a modal dialog. For a short explanation beside an export control, connect a button to the popover and provide a visible way to close it. Keep essential instructions visible in the main flow.

Connect the invoker and panel

<button type="button" popovertarget="format-help">Format help</button>
<div id="format-help" popover="auto">
  <h2>Choosing a sample format</h2>
  <p>Use the format required by the tool receiving your file.</p>
  <button type="button" popovertarget="format-help"
    popovertargetaction="hide">Close help</button>
</div>
#format-help {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  max-inline-size: min(28rem, calc(100vw - 2rem));
  padding: 1.5rem;
  border: 1px solid #aeb8c7;
  border-radius: 1rem;
}

This deliberately simple example uses the browser’s default placement. Anchoring it beside the invoker is a separate styling task. The panel contains ordinary explanatory content, so it does not claim menu semantics or require a menu’s arrow-key model.

Reference: MDN: using the Popover API.

Choose dismissal behavior intentionally

An auto popover supports light dismissal by clicking outside and browser dismissal such as Escape. Showing another unrelated auto popover generally closes the previous one. Manual popovers have different dismissal rules; switching to manual just to keep several panels open also means taking responsibility for a clear closing experience.

Popover display uses the top layer, but it does not make the rest of the document inert like a modal dialog. Avoid adding aria-modal or trapping keyboard focus merely because the panel floats above the page. Choose a modal dialog when the actual task requires a modal interaction.

Review the help journey

  • Open the panel with the keyboard and inspect the next Tab destination.
  • Close it with Escape and verify a sensible return to the invoker.
  • Use the visible close button, then reopen the panel.
  • Try long help text, zoom and a narrow viewport without clipping the close action.

Test in the browsers you support and decide what happens when the API is unavailable. For optional help, an ordinary in-flow explanation or disclosure can be an appropriate fallback. Do not hide essential content behind a button that cannot reveal it. In the handoff, record the panel’s semantics, dismissal paths, placement policy and fallback, rather than specifying only its shadow and border radius.
coverAlt: A Format help invoker and a small help panel with a visible Close help button over ordinary page content.

title: Review Your Interface in Forced Colors Mode
description: Check borders, focus indicators and selected states in forced colors mode. Use system colors for targeted repairs while preserving the user’s palette.
body:
Forced colors mode replaces parts of the page palette with colors chosen by the user and browser. A control that depends on a subtle shadow or gradient can lose its visible boundary. Review the interface in this mode and repair the missing information, while allowing the user’s palette to remain in control.

Give controls a structural boundary

.sample-action {
  border: 2px solid transparent;
  box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgb(0 0 0 / 15%);
}
.sample-action:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #174fa0;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
@media (forced-colors: active) {
  .sample-action { border-color: ButtonText; }
  .sample-action:focus-visible { outline-color: Highlight; }
}

The transparent border reserves space in the ordinary design, so exposing it in forced colors does not need to change the component’s dimensions. These system color keywords follow the active palette. Check the result with native buttons instead of assuming that a visually button-like div will receive equivalent browser treatment.

Reference: MDN: forced-colors media feature.

Inspect information that may disappear

Shadows are suppressed in forced colors, and non-URL background images such as gradients can be removed. Review boundaries, state indicators and diagrams that rely on those effects. A selected tab with only a background tint may need a visible border or another persistent indicator. Do not use a color swatch as the only label for a choice.

Avoid setting forced-color-adjust: none on an entire application to preserve brand colors. That opts content out of the user’s chosen adaptation. A narrowly scoped exception may be needed for meaningful artwork, but its purpose and readability should be reviewed independently.

Use a repeatable inspection path

  • Visit navigation, forms, dialogs and the main task flow.
  • Move keyboard focus through every interactive component.
  • Check selected, checked, disabled and error states.
  • Inspect icons and text over images as well as plain surfaces.

Use browser emulation to find likely issues, then test the relevant operating-system mode on a supported device before making broad accessibility claims. Capture the exact environment and palette used. A light palette and a dark palette can expose different assumptions in the same component.

For a useful bug report, describe the lost information: “the unselected option has no visible boundary” is more actionable than “the colors look wrong.” Attach ordinary and forced-color views of the same state, and keep repairs close to the component that needs them.
coverAlt: A standard button beside a forced-colors-style button whose border and focus outline remain visible.

title: Inspect CSS Gradient Angles and Color Stops
description: Read a linear gradient as a direction and a series of stops. Recreate smooth and hard transitions, then check the result at the component’s actual size.
body:
To reproduce a linear gradient, record its direction and stop positions as well as its colors. Two gradients with the same endpoint colors can look very different if the transition begins later or ends earlier. Inspect the full background-image declaration before sampling individual pixels from a screenshot.

Separate direction from transition length

.sample-banner {
  background-image: linear-gradient(
    90deg,
    #dceaff 0%,
    #dceaff 25%,
    #bde9d8 75%,
    #bde9d8 100%
  );
}

This original example holds pale blue through the first quarter, transitions across the middle half and finishes with pale green. At 90deg the direction runs toward the right. CSS angles start with 0deg pointing upward and increase clockwise; a graphics tool may use a different angle convention.

Reference: MDN: linear-gradient().

Recognize a hard color stop

.split-swatch {
  background-image: linear-gradient(
    to right,
    #dceaff 0% 50%,
    #bde9d8 50% 100%
  );
}

Both colors meet at 50%, producing a sharp division rather than a smooth blend. That is useful for a comparison swatch, but it is often an accidental result when a copied stop value is misplaced. Keep stop positions in the intended order and change one position at a time during diagnosis.

A gradient is an image value, so assign it to background-image or an appropriate background shorthand. It is not a background-color. Keep a plain background color underneath if the design needs a specific base, and inspect any additional background layers separately.

Review the component, not just the swatch

Test the same gradient in a tall mobile panel and a wide desktop banner. A direction toward a corner and a fixed angle can respond differently to the box’s proportions. If the source design includes a particular interpolation color space, preserve it when supported instead of assuming the midpoint will be identical in every space.

  • Record the complete gradient string and the size of the reference box.
  • Check text contrast at the least favorable part of the background.
  • Review any image or overlay composited above or below it.
  • Keep meaningful labels visible if the decorative gradient disappears.

In the handoff, name what the gradient does: surface decoration, image scrim or comparison graphic. That purpose determines whether a slight visual difference is acceptable or whether the exact stop structure carries information.
coverAlt: A smooth blue-to-green gradient holds each end color through a quarter of its width, compared with a sharp halfway split.

title: Use CSS color-mix() for Related Surface Tokens
description: Derive a related interface surface with color-mix(). Choose the color space, keep a fallback and validate contrast instead of treating a mix as a guarantee.
body:
color-mix() can express a relationship between a brand color and a surface color directly in CSS. That can make a token easier to maintain than a disconnected hex value. The relationship still needs visual and contrast review: mixing a fixed percentage of blue into white does not automatically produce an accessible text or control color.

Create one derived surface

:root {
  --brand: #245ec7;
  --canvas: #ffffff;
  --note-surface: #eef3fb;
}
@supports (color: color-mix(in oklab, black, white)) {
  :root {
    --note-surface: color-mix(in oklab, var(--brand) 10%, var(--canvas));
  }
}
.note { background: var(--note-surface); color: #17263f; }

The fallback is an independently chosen light surface, not a claim that it exactly equals the calculated mix. The supports condition matters because a custom property can hold an unsupported function as text; simply placing an older custom-property value before a newer one is not always a useful feature fallback.

Reference: MDN: color-mix().

Name the color relationship

The example mixes in Oklab and gives the brand a 10% contribution, with the remaining contribution assigned to the canvas color. Another color space can produce a different intermediate color. Record the space with the percentages so a later conversion to a static token does not silently change the result.

Mixing with transparent also affects alpha and therefore depends on the eventual background. Mixing with white produces a different relationship. If the same token is used over several surfaces, inspect the composed result in each location rather than comparing only a color picker’s raw value.

Keep semantic roles explicit

A note surface, a border and a text color have different requirements. Do not derive all three with one percentage because it keeps the token file short. Start with the surface relationship, then choose readable foreground and boundary treatments for the actual component.

  • Change the brand color to a much lighter and a much darker sample.
  • Review the component on each supported theme.
  • Measure contrast using the colors that are actually rendered together.
  • Check the fallback with the supports block disabled.

For handoff, include the semantic token name, its formula and the components that use it. When a theme changes the canvas token, repeat the review instead of assuming the original mixing percentage remains suitable. The formula communicates intent; it does not replace validation.
coverAlt: A brand-color swatch and white canvas swatch feed a derived note surface labeled with its mixing relationship.

title: Align Numeric Columns with CSS Tabular Numerals
description: Use tabular-nums for stable number columns and counters. Check font support, decimal formatting and alignment without changing the rest of your typography.
body:
When digits shift inside a counter or look uneven in a numeric column, try tabular numerals in a font that supports them. The digits receive equal advance widths, while surrounding text can keep the site’s normal proportional typeface. This is different from switching the entire interface to a monospace font.

Apply the feature to the numeric cells

<table class="sample-totals">
  <caption>Illustrative file totals</caption>
  <thead><tr><th scope="col">Group</th><th scope="col">Files</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><th scope="row">Icons</th><td class="number">111</td></tr>
    <tr><th scope="row">Images</th><td class="number">888</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
.number {
  font-variant-numeric: lining-nums tabular-nums;
  text-align: end;
}

The sample values are deliberately different digit shapes. Compare their widths with the feature enabled and disabled. The chosen font must contain the relevant glyph variants; a CSS declaration cannot create a missing OpenType feature.

Reference: MDN: font-variant-numeric.

Separate digit width from number formatting

Tabular digits do not align decimal points in arbitrarily formatted strings. Values such as 9.5 and 12.50 still have different numbers of decimal places. Decide on a consistent display precision when the data allows it, and choose an alignment that suits the comparison. Do not add misleading trailing precision to measurements merely to make the table look tidy.

Currency symbols, minus signs and separators can have their own widths. Test the full formatted value, including negative numbers and the longest expected amount. A right-aligned column can help scanning, but it does not fix an unclear unit or an inconsistent formatting policy.

Check dynamic and fallback states

For a countdown or status counter, compare repeated transitions such as 11 to 88. If the number gains another digit, the overall string still grows; reserve an appropriate width only when the range is known. Avoid clipping a larger value just because the original mockup contained two digits.

  • Inspect the rendered font, including any fallback used before loading completes.
  • Compare ordinary digits, tabular digits and the actual production weight.
  • Check zoom and the narrow table layout.
  • Keep column headers and units associated with their values.

Document the feature on the numeric text style, not as a global rule for every paragraph. Proportional numerals may remain a better fit for running prose. The goal is stable comparison where it helps the reader, without flattening the typography of the whole page.
coverAlt: A numeric table aligns illustrative file counts in equal-width digit columns while labels keep proportional typography.

title: Spot Faux Bold and Italic with CSS font-synthesis
description: Diagnose synthetic bold or italic text. Inspect the loaded faces and font declarations before deciding whether to disable synthesis for a type specimen.
keyword: css font synthesis faux bold italic
body:
A heading can look heavier than its intended font because the browser is synthesizing a missing bold face. Italic text can similarly be slanted from an upright face. Before changing letter spacing or choosing another font, check whether the requested weight and style actually have a matching font resource.

Create a focused comparison

<p class="type-sample">Regular <strong>Bold</strong> <em>Italic</em></p>
.type-sample { font-family: "Project Sans", sans-serif; }
/* Diagnostic toggle: compare both settings. */
.type-sample { font-synthesis: none; }

Use the real project family in this specimen. Toggle synthesis only while watching the rendered faces and network requests. If the appearance changes, investigate the missing face. Disabling synthesis does not download or create the correct bold or italic design.

Reference: MDN: font-synthesis.

Check the font declarations

@font-face {
  font-family: "Project Sans";
  src: url("/fonts/project-bold.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 700;
  font-style: normal;
  font-display: swap;
}

This is a declaration pattern for a real file you supply. The weight and style descriptors should describe that file accurately. A regular file labeled as 700 is not a substitute for a designed bold face. For a variable font, declare its actual supported range and inspect whether the requested style has its own resource or axis.

Check the request status, response type and rendered-font information. A successful response alone does not prove the intended face is used on every glyph. Missing character coverage can cause part of a phrase to fall back to another family, making the problem look inconsistent.

Decide where synthesis should remain available

For a tightly controlled brand specimen, disabling synthesis can expose missing assets during review. For broad reading content, a global prohibition deserves more care because fallback fonts may not include every requested style. Review emphasis and hierarchy in loading and failure states before applying the setting across the entire site.

  • Compare regular, bold, italic and bold italic in the actual text size.
  • Include accented characters and symbols used by the content.
  • Simulate a font load failure and inspect the fallback.
  • Check that strong and emphasized text remain understandable.

Record the family, face files, supported weights and synthesis policy in the typography handoff. A screenshot of the final heading is useful, but the resource mapping is what makes the result reproducible on another machine.
coverAlt: A font resource checklist separates a real regular face, bold face and italic face before synthesis is disabled.

title: text-wrap: balance vs pretty for Headings and Copy
description: Compare balanced headings with improved paragraph wrapping. Apply text-wrap selectively and test real fonts, narrow widths and changing content.
body:
Use text-wrap: balance to improve the distribution of a short heading across lines. Consider text-wrap: pretty for selected reading text where the browser can favor a better line arrangement. Neither value replaces a sensible text width, font size or content edit, and exact line breaks can vary by browser and font.

Start with a stable text measure

.feature-heading {
  max-inline-size: 20ch;
  text-wrap: balance;
}
.feature-intro {
  max-inline-size: 60ch;
  text-wrap: pretty;
}

Try the heading “Inspect the details behind a better interface” with your actual typeface. Compare the default wrapping and balanced wrapping at several widths. A 20ch measure is an illustrative starting point, not a universal headline width; ch itself depends on the selected font’s metrics.

Reference: MDN: text-wrap.

Choose the property for the content

Balancing is intended for short blocks, and browsers limit how many lines they balance. Pretty wrapping gives the browser room to improve the layout of text, but its precise algorithm and support can differ. Apply these as progressive enhancements: the copy should remain readable with ordinary wrapping.

Do not insert hard line breaks solely to reproduce a desktop screenshot if the same heading must adapt to mobile widths. A forced break can make a narrow layout worse. Keep intentional breaks for cases where the content or design genuinely requires them and test those separately.

Review the states that alter line breaks

  • Check before and after the web font loads.
  • Use the shortest and longest real heading examples.
  • Test narrow cards as well as full-width sections.
  • Zoom text and inspect the heading’s relationship to nearby controls.

If the last word still looks stranded, first inspect the text measure and wording. Adding balance to a container with a fixed height may reveal a different problem: the heading can gain a line and collide with the next element. Let content determine block height instead of relying on the original line count.

For long bodies of text, evaluate the tradeoff before applying pretty everywhere. Use it where the typographic benefit is visible and the page remains responsive with realistic content. A page full of short UI labels does not need the same treatment as an editorial introduction.

In design handoff, specify the maximum measure and wrapping preference without requiring one exact set of line endings on every device. That gives the implementation room to respect reader settings while keeping the intended hierarchy.
coverAlt: A short heading is shown with balanced line lengths beside a paragraph with a deliberate readable measure.

title: Use image-set() for Sharp CSS Backgrounds
description: Offer standard and high-density CSS background images with image-set(). Keep a fallback, verify asset dimensions and inspect the browser’s selected request.
body:
Use image-set() to offer multiple resolutions of a decorative CSS background. It gives the browser candidates rather than forcing the largest file onto every device. When the image communicates information that needs alternative text, use appropriate HTML image markup instead of moving that content into a background.

Prepare two versions of the same artwork

.texture-panel {
  background-image: url("/images/paper-1x.webp");
  background-image: image-set(
    url("/images/paper-1x.webp") 1x,
    url("/images/paper-2x.webp") 2x
  );
  background-size: 320px 200px;
  background-repeat: repeat;
}

For this illustrative repeating texture, prepare a 320 by 200 pixel base asset and a 640 by 400 pixel high-density asset with the same composition. Both represent the same 320 by 200 CSS-pixel tile. Replace the paths with actual project files before using the example.

Reference: MDN: image-set().

Keep resolution and composition separate

A 2x candidate should provide more image detail for the same intended appearance. If it also changes the crop or moves a decorative mark, switching candidates will change the design. Use a deliberate art-direction strategy when the composition itself needs to change at a breakpoint.

The earlier background-image declaration provides a plain-image fallback. Supporting browsers can choose an image-set candidate based on device and environment. Do not assume that a particular device pixel ratio always proves one exact file must be selected; inspect the actual network request.

Verify selection and visual size

  • Check that both files return successfully and have the intended pixel dimensions.
  • Inspect the requested background file in the Network panel.
  • Compare the tile’s visible CSS size across density settings.
  • Look for seams and compression artifacts in the high-density version.

Use a fresh load when evaluating selection and account for caching. A previously loaded candidate can make a quick experiment misleading. Record the viewport, density setting and requested file in the review evidence instead of judging only from a screenshot.

If the design uses background-size: cover, also test the crop in the actual element proportions. Extra resolution cannot restore content that cover crops away. For large decorative photography, review file weight as well as sharpness; the high-density candidate should earn its transfer cost at the size people actually see.

Document the logical display size, each source’s pixel dimensions and the asset’s decorative role. That prevents a later export from silently changing the scale of the background pattern.
coverAlt: Standard and high-density texture assets have different pixel dimensions but share the same CSS display size.

title: Style Native Checkboxes with CSS accent-color
description: Apply a brand tint to native form controls with accent-color. Preserve their behavior and review labels, focus, disabled states and browser differences.
body:
If a checkbox only needs a different tint, try accent-color before rebuilding it from custom elements. Supporting browsers can apply the color while retaining the native control’s interaction. Treat the result as a browser-rendered control, not a promise of identical pixels on every platform.

Keep the input and label connected

<label class="export-option">
  <input type="checkbox" name="include-notes" checked>
  Include review notes
</label>
.export-option {
  display: flex;
  align-items: start;
  gap: .6rem;
}
.export-option input { accent-color: #245ec7; }
.export-option input:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #174fa0;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

The wrapping label connects the visible wording to the input and gives it a larger activation area. Keep the real input visible. This example changes its tint without using appearance: none, hiding it behind a pseudo-element or replacing the native checked state with a CSS class.

Reference: MDN: accent-color.

Know the scope of the property

The property applies to certain native controls and relevant states, such as checked checkboxes, radio buttons and portions of range or progress controls in supporting browsers. It is not a general way to recolor every part of every form element. An unsupported browser can retain its ordinary native appearance.

If the unchecked border does not match a mockup, that does not necessarily mean the declaration failed. Inspect the selected state and compare the browser’s control styling. Avoid layering increasingly broad selectors onto the page to chase a part the property does not control.

Review the full option row

  • Toggle with the keyboard and by clicking the label.
  • Check the focus ring on both light and dark surrounding surfaces.
  • Inspect checked, unchecked and disabled states.
  • Test long labels that wrap to two lines at a narrow width.

Use a real form when checking submission: the visual checkmark and the submitted value are related but separate concerns. Confirm the input has the intended name and value in the application. Do not imply that changing its tint changes how validation or form data works.

Review forced colors and supported operating systems as part of the component check. Native controls can adapt to user preferences, so avoid rejecting that adaptation simply because it differs from the brand screenshot. In the handoff, define the intended accent, label spacing and interaction requirements, while allowing platform-specific rendering where it remains clear and usable.
coverAlt: A checked native-style option with a blue accent and a clear label, beside an unchecked option.

title: Capture DevTools CSS Edits Before They Disappear
description: Use Chrome’s Changes panel to review temporary CSS edits, copy the relevant changes into source and confirm that a clean reload preserves the intended fix.
body:
A CSS adjustment in DevTools is usually an experiment until it has been transferred to the project source. Use the Changes panel to review what changed before reloading. Then apply the useful part to the correct stylesheet or component and verify the result from a clean build.

Make one reviewable experiment

Imagine a card whose label sits too close to its icon. Inspect the row and change its gap from 8px to 12px. Avoid changing padding, font size and line height at the same time. One focused experiment gives you a clear before-and-after result and a small change to transfer.

  • Open DevTools and make the CSS edit in Elements > Styles.
  • Open the Command Menu and choose Show Changes.
  • Select the affected file and review its diff.
  • Copy the relevant CSS changes before reloading the page.

Reference: Chrome DevTools: Changes panel.

Move the intent into the right source file

/* Example source-level change after review */
.card-label {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: .75rem;
}

This specimen expresses a 12px gap at a 16px root font size. If your project uses a spacing token, use the corresponding approved token instead of adding a new literal. If the inspected CSS is generated or minified, find the component, utility or source stylesheet that owns the rule. Editing the generated output alone may be lost at the next build.

The Changes panel tracks edits made within DevTools; it is not a project-wide version-control diff. Ordinary temporary edits can disappear on reload. Local overrides can persist a browser-side experiment, while Workspaces can connect edits to local source files. Choose the mechanism deliberately and verify where a change is actually saved.

Confirm the source now owns the result

Rebuild the project, remove or disable any local override used during investigation, and reload. If the fix disappears, the browser experiment may still be the only place it exists. Check the source diff and the served stylesheet rather than making another temporary edit to hide the problem.

  • Test another component instance using the same class.
  • Check a narrow viewport and a longer label.
  • Review hover and keyboard focus if the row is interactive.
  • Keep unrelated experimental changes out of the final commit.

For handoff, attach the small source diff and a screenshot of the corrected state. Include the reason for the change, such as preventing an icon from crowding a wrapped label. A copied CSS block without that context is harder for the next developer to evaluate.
coverAlt: An illustrative CSS diff changes an eight-pixel gap to twelve pixels, then transfers the reviewed change to source.

title: Use Chrome Coverage Without Deleting Needed CSS
description: Investigate unused CSS with DevTools Coverage. Record interactive states, distinguish unobserved rules from dead code and verify removals across routes.
body:
Chrome’s Coverage panel shows which parts of a loaded resource were used during the recorded session. Unused in that session does not mean safe to delete from the application. A menu, error state or responsive layout may need rules that your first page load never exercised.

Record a task, not only a screenshot

  • Open DevTools, then use the Command Menu to show Coverage.
  • Start the reload-and-record action.
  • Perform the page’s main interactions while recording continues.
  • Open a CSS resource to inspect the used and unused regions.

Reference: Chrome DevTools: Coverage.

For a sample export page, open its options, trigger a validation error with harmless sample input, dismiss the error and complete the preview flow. Repeat at the relevant responsive widths. Write down the path you exercised so the report has a defined scope.

Classify an unused rule before removing it

/* Example investigation notes, not a deletion list */
.export-error   -> only visible after failed validation
.mobile-tools   -> only displayed at narrow widths
.legacy-banner  -> no current template reference found

The first two candidates need additional state coverage. The third may deserve a source search, but a missing template match is still only evidence: classes can be generated dynamically or supplied by content. Trace the component owner and route usage before deciding the rule is obsolete.

A shared stylesheet can serve several pages. Recording one route does not establish that its unused rules are unnecessary elsewhere. Likewise, print styles, theme rules and interaction selectors may have conditions outside your initial session. Keep those conditions in the review notes rather than treating a single percentage as a site-wide verdict.

Make a small, reversible cleanup

Remove only a well-understood set of obsolete rules in source. Rebuild and exercise the routes and states that previously depended on the file. Compare the resulting resource size and behavior. Do not claim a loading-speed improvement from a smaller unused percentage alone; performance requires its own measurement.

  • Check the component’s normal, loading, empty and error states.
  • Review the widest and narrowest supported layouts.
  • Inspect keyboard focus and open overlays.
  • Confirm that production builds preserve dynamically used classes.

For handoff, include the recording scope, candidate rules, source ownership and validation performed. That turns Coverage into an investigation tool instead of an automatic deletion instruction. The useful outcome is a stylesheet with a clearer purpose and no lost interface states, not merely a greener report.
coverAlt: A coverage review separates an error-state rule, a mobile rule and a possible legacy rule before deciding what to remove.

title: Inspect Hover and Focus Styles in Chrome DevTools
description: Freeze CSS interaction states in DevTools to inspect their styles. Separate a forced pseudo-class from real keyboard focus, pointer events and application behavior.
body:
Forcing a pseudo-class in DevTools makes a CSS state easier to inspect without holding the pointer in place. It is useful for comparing a hover color or focus outline. It does not replace testing the real interaction, especially when JavaScript, keyboard order or touch behavior determines what appears.

Freeze the styling you want to inspect

  • Select the target element in the Elements panel.
  • In Styles, open the :hov state controls.
  • Enable the relevant state, such as :hover or :focus-visible.
  • Inspect the winning declarations and compare with the ordinary state.

Reference: Chrome DevTools: CSS features reference.

.sample-link { color: #174fa0; text-decoration: underline; }
.sample-link:hover { color: #102f65; }
.sample-link:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}

This original link example makes hover and keyboard-focus styling independent. Toggle one state at a time, then inspect the combination. If the focus outline disappears when hover is active, check rule order and shorthand resets rather than assuming the browser cannot display both.

Separate styling from behavior

Forcing :hover does not necessarily execute the pointer event handlers that open a custom panel. Forcing :focus does not prove that the element can be reached in the page’s Tab sequence. If the application adds a class after an event, inspect that class-based state as well and reproduce the actual event path.

A parent’s :focus-within can change a whole field group while the input holds real focus. Select the relevant ancestor when investigating that relationship. Also check whether an overlay, disabled control or clipping container changes what the user can interact with, even when the CSS declarations look correct.

Finish with an unforced interaction pass

  • Clear the forced states so they cannot mask the real result.
  • Tab through the page and check focus order and visibility.
  • Use the pointer to enter, leave, press and release the control.
  • Try the interface without hover on a touch-capable device.

For a dropdown, verify opening, moving into the panel, activating an item and closing again. A beautiful frozen hover screenshot can hide a gap that makes the menu collapse as the pointer travels. Capture the trigger and path when reporting that bug.

In the handoff, label screenshots with the inspected state and say whether it was forced or reached through interaction. That distinction helps another developer reproduce the visual evidence and understand which behavior still needs testing.
coverAlt: Three link states show a regular underline, a hover color and a visible focus outline, followed by a reminder to test real interaction.
